q.v: A researcher is studying the conversion of succinate to fumarate by succinate dehydrogenase in isolated mitochondria. When the substrate binds to the active site, the enzyme lowers the activation energy of the reaction by a specific amount, Delta G_B. Which of the following molecular events directly accounts for the generation of this Delta G_B and the resulting rate enhancement?
o: Covalent modification of the substrate by inorganic phosphate
Alteration of the ground state free energy of the final fumarate product
Formation of bonds between the substrate and enzyme functional groups alongside desolvation
Spontaneous increase in ambient reaction temperature within the active site cleft
Consumption of high-energy ATP molecules to force reactant collisions
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that lowering activation energy by Delta G_B requires the system to gain an equivalent amount of energy during transition state stabilization) -> Step 2 (Conclude that Delta G_B arises from bonds formed between substrate and enzyme functional groups, fixing geometry and removing shielding water/desolvation)

r.A: Adding inorganic phosphate describes the mechanism of a phosphorylase rather than the general thermodynamic origin of binding energy (Delta G_B).
r.B: Catalysts lower the activation energy required to reach the transition state without altering the ground state free energy of the substrate or product.
r.D: While higher temperatures yield more effective collisions in uncatalyzed reactions, enzymes enhance rates by fixing geometry and desolvation rather than raising temperature.
r.E: The conversion of succinate to fumarate and general transition state stabilization by Delta G_B do not require ATP hydrolysis to force collisions.

q.s: Slide 4: Catalysts Lower the Amount of Energy S Needs to Reach Transition State & Slide 5: Enzymes Provide Substrate Specificity and Rate Enhancement

q.v: A 48-year-old man presents to the clinic with progressive fatigue, pallor, and scaling skin lesions. Bone marrow aspirate reveals ringed sideroblasts, confirming a diagnosis of sideroblastic anemia. The physician prescribes high-dose supplementation of a specific water-soluble vitamin to restore the function of a defective coenzyme. Which of the following biochemical processes is most directly dependent on the vitamin deficient in this patient?
o: Pyruvate dehydrogenase and transketolase reactions
Heme synthesis and amino acid modification
Transfer of CO2 groups in fatty acid metabolism
DNA synthesis and fatty acid metabolism
Precursor synthesis for coenzyme A (CoA)
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the presentation of skin disorders and sideroblastic anemia as a deficiency of Vitamin B6 / pyridoxine) -> Step 2 (Connect Vitamin B6 to its key biochemical roles in heme synthesis and amino acid synthesis/modification)

r.A: Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) and transketolase (TK) require Vitamin B1 (thiamine), whose deficiency causes beriberi.
r.C: Transferring CO2 groups in fatty acid, amino acid, and carbohydrate metabolism requires Vitamin B7 (biotin), which can be bound up by raw egg whites.
r.D: DNA synthesis and fatty acid metabolism are key reactions for Vitamin B12 (cobalamin), whose deficiency leads to megaloblastic anemia and neurological damage.
r.E: Serving as a precursor to CoA is the function of Vitamin B5 (pantothenic acid), whose rare deficiency causes fatigue and numbness.

q.s: Slide 8: B Vitamin Overview

q.v: A 6-month-old infant is evaluated for severe fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly. Liver biopsy demonstrates a complete deficiency of the enzyme responsible for converting glucose-6-phosphate into free glucose and inorganic phosphate during gluconeogenesis, reversing the irreversible step catalyzed by hexokinase. Based on enzyme classification terminology, which of the following describes the specific mechanism of the deficient enzyme?
o: Transfers a phosphate group from ATP onto glucose-6-phosphate
Adds an inorganic phosphate molecule onto the substrate without using ATP
Removes a phosphate group from the substrate without generating ATP
Relocates the phosphate functional group from carbon-6 to carbon-1 within the molecule
Joins glucose and phosphate together utilizing the energy of acetyl-CoA
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the deficient gluconeogenic enzyme converting glucose-6-phosphate to free glucose as Glucose-6-Phosphatase) -> Step 2 (Apply enzyme terminology to define a phosphatase as an enzyme that removes a phosphate group from a substrate)

r.A: Transferring a phosphate group from a high-energy molecule like ATP onto a substrate defines a kinase, such as hexokinase.
r.B: Adding inorganic phosphate onto a substrate without using ATP or GTP defines a phosphorylase, such as glycogen phosphorylase.
r.D: Relocating a functional group within a single molecule defines a mutase (a type of isomerase), such as bisphosphoglycerate mutase.
r.E: Joining two molecules together using an energy source like ATP or acetyl-CoA defines a synthase or synthetase.

q.s: Slide 10: Enzyme Terminology & Slide 13: Phosphatase

q.v: An investigator is studying erythrocyte glycolysis and isolates the enzyme responsible for converting 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate into 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate. In a separate experiment, the investigator studies a mitochondrial enzyme that converts L-malate to oxaloacetate while reducing NAD+ to NADH. Which of the following correctly pairs the enzyme classification for the erythrocyte enzyme and the mitochondrial enzyme, respectively?
o: Kinase and Hydrolase
Phosphorylase and Carboxylase
Mutase and Dehydrogenase
Synthetase and Hydroxylase
Phosphatase and Mutase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the intramolecular rearrangement of 1,3-BPG to 2,3-BPG as catalyzed by Bisphosphoglycerate Mutase, and the oxidation-reduction of L-malate to oxaloacetate removing hydrogen as catalyzed by L-malate dehydrogenase) -> Step 2 (Pair Mutase and Dehydrogenase accordingly)

r.A: A kinase transfers phosphate from ATP, while a hydrolase adds H2O to a chemical bond (such as cyclic AMP phosphodiesterase).
r.B: A phosphorylase adds inorganic phosphate without ATP, while a carboxylase transfers CO2 groups utilizing biotin.
r.D: A synthetase joins two molecules using an energy source (such as glycine-tRNA ligase), while a hydroxylase adds an -OH group onto a substrate.
r.E: A phosphatase removes a phosphate group from a substrate, whereas the mitochondrial reaction involves electron transfer and hydrogen depletion via a dehydrogenase.

q.s: Slide 14: Dehydrogenases & Slide 17: Mutase (type of isomerase)

q.v: A biochemist measures the initial reaction velocity (v) of a newly isolated enzyme across several substrate concentrations [S]. At [S] = 1 mM, v = 0.8 micromoles/liter/min; at [S] = 5 mM, v = 2.0 micromoles/liter/min; at [S] = 10 mM, v = 3.0 micromoles/liter/min; at [S] = 20 mM, v = 4.0 micromoles/liter/min; and at [S] = 50 mM, v = 5.0 micromoles/liter/min (where the curve plateaus). If a non-competitive antagonist is added to this reaction mixture, which of the following changes will occur to the kinetic parameters of this enzyme?
o: The apparent Km will increase above 7.5 mM, while Vmax remains at 5.0 micromoles/liter/min
The apparent Vmax will decrease below 5.0 micromoles/liter/min, while Km remains unchanged
Both the apparent Vmax and the apparent Km will increase proportionally
The apparent Km will decrease below 5.0 mM, while Vmax decreases below 2.5 micromoles/liter/min
The enzyme will transition from hyperbolic kinetics to sigmoidal kinetics with an unchanged Vmax
q.p: Step 1 (Determine from the table that Vmax plateaus at 5.0 micromoles/liter/min and 1/2 Vmax is 2.5 micromoles/liter/min, corresponding to a baseline Km between 5 and 10 mM) -> Step 2 (Apply the mechanism of non-competitive inhibition, which distorts the enzyme to slow product formation, decreasing apparent Vmax below 5.0 without altering Km)

r.A: An increase in apparent Km without a change in Vmax is characteristic of a reversible competitive inhibitor, not a non-competitive inhibitor.
r.C: Non-competitive antagonists decrease the apparent Vmax and do not change the Km.
r.D: Neither competitive nor non-competitive inhibition causes a decrease in Km alongside a decreased Vmax in Michaelis-Menten kinetics.
r.E: Sigmoidal kinetics are characteristic of multimeric allosteric enzymes rather than standard Michaelis-Menten enzymes exposed to a non-competitive antagonist.

q.s: Slide 23: Substrate Concentration vs Velocity Graph & Slide 25: Non-Competitive Inhibition

q.v: During an experiment on intracellular signaling pathways, a pharmacologist treats a hepatocyte culture with a compound that selectively inhibits transcription factors regulating the gene expression of MAP kinase, reducing the total number of MAP kinase enzyme molecules in the cells by 50%. Assuming no allosteric effectors or covalent modifications are introduced, how will this transcriptional downregulation affect the intracellular kinetic parameters of the MAP kinase reaction?
o: Decreased Km with an unchanged Vmax
Increased Km with an unchanged Vmax
Decreased Vmax with an unchanged Km
Increased Vmax with a decreased Km
Unchanged Vmax and unchanged Km
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that transcriptional downregulation decreases the total concentration/number of enzyme molecules available in the tissue) -> Step 2 (Deduce that fewer enzyme molecules reduces the maximal velocity [Vmax] of the system without altering the intrinsic substrate affinity [Km] of the remaining individual enzymes)

r.A: Km is an intrinsic property of the enzyme's active site affinity for its substrate and does not decrease when enzyme concentration drops.
r.B: An increased Km indicates lower affinity (such as in competitive inhibition), which does not occur simply from having fewer enzyme molecules.
r.D: Reducing the number of enzyme molecules decreases, rather than increases, the maximum possible reaction rate (Vmax).
r.E: Because Vmax is directly proportional to the total amount of active enzyme present, decreasing enzyme quantity must decrease Vmax.

q.s: Slide 28: Examples of Regulation of Enzyme Activity & Slide 50: Enzymes 4

q.v: A 28-year-old sprinter is in the middle of a 100-meter dash, causing rapid consumption of cellular ATP and a sharp rise in intracellular AMP concentrations within his skeletal myocytes. How does this elevated AMP concentration alter the kinetic behavior of phosphofructokinase I (PFK-1) to regulate central metabolism?
o: It binds to the active site as a substrate to directly phosphorylate fructose-6-phosphate
It acts as a heterotropic positive allosteric effector, shifting the sigmoidal velocity curve to the left
It irreversibly cleaves a peptide bond on PFK-1 to expose the catalytic cleft
It phosphorylates a serine residue on PFK-1 to disrupt internal electrostatic bonds
It acts as a negative allosteric effector, increasing the K0.5 for fructose-6-phosphate
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize PFK-1 as a multimeric allosteric enzyme in glycolysis that produces fructose-1,6-bisphosphate and is allosterically activated by AMP) -> Step 2 (Conclude that as a positive heterotropic effector, AMP shifts the sigmoidal rate curve to the left, decreasing Km/K0.5 and increasing reaction velocity at lower fructose-6-P concentrations)

r.A: ATP, not AMP, serves as the high-energy phosphate donor substrate for kinases like PFK-1.
r.C: Irreversible proteolytic cleavage describes zymogen activation (such as pepsinogen to pepsin), whereas AMP regulates PFK-1 noncovalently.
r.D: Phosphorylation of serine residues is a reversible covalent modification mediated by protein kinases (like PKA), not by noncovalent AMP binding.
r.E: ATP, not AMP, acts as the negative allosteric effector of PFK-1 that shifts the curve to the right and increases K0.5.

q.s: Slide 27: Allosteric Enzymes: Heterotropic Effects & Slide 31: Phosphofructokinase I: A Model of Allosteric Regulation by Physiologic Effectors

q.v: A 42-year-old man consumes a high-protein meal, stimulating parietal cells in his gastric glands to secrete hydrochloric acid (HCl) and chief cells to secrete pepsinogen into the stomach lumen. Which of the following mechanisms directly converts the inactive pepsinogen into active pepsin within the gastric lumen?
o: Reversible phosphorylation of a serine residue by cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA)
Allosteric activation via binding of free amino acids to a regulatory subunit
Low pH-induced disruption of electrostatic bonds leading to irreversible autocatalytic cleavage
Dephosphorylation of the enzyme by an insulin-stimulated phosphoprotein phosphatase
Addition of water across a cyclic phosphodiester bond by a specific hydrolase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify pepsinogen as an inactive zymogen secreted by gastric chief cells into the low-pH environment created by parietal cell HCl) -> Step 2 (Determine that low pH alters the electrostatic interactions holding the inhibitory peptide in place, resulting in irreversible covalent modification via autocatalytic cleavage to pepsin)

r.A: Reversible phosphorylation by PKA regulates intracellular metabolic enzymes like phosphorylase kinase and glycogen synthase, not luminal gastric zymogens.
r.B: Zymogen activation is an irreversible covalent modification via proteolytic processing, not a reversible noncovalent allosteric regulation.
r.D: Insulin-stimulated phosphatases regulate intracellular glycogen metabolism via reversible dephosphorylation, not gastric protein digestion.
r.E: Hydrolysis of a cyclic phosphodiester bond describes the conversion of cAMP to 5' AMP by cyclic AMP phosphodiesterase.

q.s: Slide 33: Organs and Locale of Protein Digestion & Slide 34: Activation of Pepsinogen to Pepsin

q.v: A 19-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus administers her mealtime insulin injection after consuming a carbohydrate-rich meal. In her hepatocytes, insulin signaling counteracts the effects of glucagon and PKA by activating phosphoprotein phosphatases. Which of the following sets of enzymatic changes will directly result from this phosphatase activation?
o: Activation of glycogen synthase and inactivation of glycogen phosphorylase
Activation of phosphorylase kinase and activation of glycogen phosphorylase
Phosphorylation of CREB and increased transcription of gluconeogenic enzymes
Inactivation of glycogen synthase and increased conversion of glycogen to glucose
Disruption of serine electrostatic bonds via addition of negatively charged phosphate groups
q.p: Step 1 (Trace that glucagon/PKA phosphorylates glycogen synthase to inactivate it and phosphorylates phosphorylase kinase to activate glycogen phosphorylase) -> Step 2 (Deduce that insulin-activated phosphatases remove these phosphate groups, thereby activating glycogen synthase to store glucose and inactivating phosphorylase kinase/glycogen phosphorylase)

r.B: Phosphorylase kinase and glycogen phosphorylase are activated when phosphorylated by PKA under glucagon signaling, whereas phosphatases inactivate them.
r.C: PKA activates CREB by phosphorylating it to increase expression of glucose transporters and gluconeogenic enzymes; phosphatases reverse phosphorylation.
r.D: Inactivation of glycogen synthase and mobilization of glycogen to glucose is the result of PKA-mediated phosphorylation, not phosphatase activity.
r.E: Adding a negatively charged phosphate group to serine to disrupt electrostatic bonds is the mechanism of a protein kinase, whereas a phosphatase removes the phosphate group.

q.s: Slide 38: Protein Phosphorylation Alters Protein Conformation and Function & Slide 40: Reversible covalent modification

q.v: A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe, crushing substernal chest pain that began 14 hours ago. Serum laboratory testing reveals a marked elevation in cardiac troponin (at its peak level) alongside an elevated creatine phosphokinase isozyme that specifically refines energy metabolism for cardiac tissue. Compared to the creatine phosphokinase isozymes predominantly found in skeletal muscle and brain tissue, which of the following characteristics is shared by all three of these isozymes?
o: They are encoded at the exact same genetic locus on a single chromosome
They possess identical amino acid sequences and identical electrophoretic mobilities
They catalyze the exact same biochemical reaction despite having different amino acid sequences
They exhibit identical Michaelis constants (Km) and identical allosteric regulatory features
They function primarily as nuclear transcription factors until released by myocyte necrosis
q.p: Step 1 (Identify CK-MB [heart], CK-MM [skeletal muscle], and CK-BB [brain/smooth muscle] as isozymes of creatine phosphokinase released into the blood during tissue damage) -> Step 2 (Apply the definition of isozymes as a group of enzymes with differing amino acid sequences that catalyze the exact same reaction)

r.A: Isozymes are encoded at different genetic loci rather than the same genetic locus.
r.B: Isozymes have differing amino acid sequences and display physical differences such as distinct electrophoretic mobilities.
r.D: Each member of an isozyme group may have a characteristic, distinct Km and/or regulatory feature to refine metabolism for specific tissue demands.
r.E: Isozymes are catalytic enzymes that refine tissue metabolism, whereas transcription factors (such as CREB) bind DNA to regulate gene expression.

q.s: Slide 43: Isozymes & Slide 45: Myocardial Infarction

q.v: A biochemist is studying the thermodynamic profile of a spontaneous metabolic reaction in an isolated hepatocyte extract. To accelerate the rate of product formation without increasing the ambient temperature of the fragile cellular proteins, the researcher introduces a purified enzyme specific to the reactant. Which of the following physical processes occurs within the enzyme's active site to directly reduce the energy required for the substrate to reach the transition state?
o: Increasing the free energy of the product ground state
Removing shielding water molecules via desolvation
Making the overall reaction free energy change more negative
Preventing the physical collision of reactant molecules
Raising the energy barrier between the ground state and transition state
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that catalysts/enzymes accelerate reactions by lowering the transition state activation energy, Delta G double-dagger) -> Step 2 (Determine that catalysts achieve this by fixing substrate geometry and removing shielding water [desolvation] to increase effective collisions and concentrate energy).

r.A: Catalysts do not alter the free energy of the ground states of either substrates or products.
r.C: Enzymes lower the activation energy required to reach the transition state but do not alter the overall free energy change (Delta G) of the reaction.
r.D: Chemical reactions require reactant molecules to collide with enough energy to react, and catalysts increase rather than prevent effective collisions.
r.E: Enzymes lower, rather than raise, the amount of energy needed to raise the substrate from the low-energy ground state to the high-energy transition state.

q.s: Slide 4: Catalysts Lower the Amount of Energy S Needs to Reach Transition State (SLO 1)

q.v: A 54-year-old man with a history of severe chronic malnutrition presents to the clinic with progressive memory impairment, symmetric peripheral neuropathy, and a macrocytic anemia characterized by hypersegmented neutrophils. Laboratory evaluation confirms a severe deficiency in a water-soluble B vitamin that is required as a cofactor for both DNA synthesis and fatty acid metabolism. Which of the following additional clinical or biochemical features is most specifically associated with a deficiency in a different B vitamin that participates in DNA/RNA synthesis and amino acid metabolism, rather than fatty acid metabolism?
o: Fetal neural tube defects
Pellagra characterized by the 4 Ds
Beriberi with impaired pyruvate dehydrogenase activity
Ariboflavinosis presenting with sore throat and dermatitis
Alopecia and dermatitis induced by raw egg white consumption
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the patient's presentation of megaloblastic anemia and neurological damage due to deficiency of B12/cobalamin, which functions in DNA synthesis and fatty acid metabolism) -> Step 2 (Contrast with B9/folate, which functions in DNA/RNA synthesis and amino acid metabolism, and whose deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neural tube defects).

r.B: Pellagra is caused by a deficiency of vitamin B3 (niacin), which serves as a precursor for NAD/NADH and NADP/NADPH.
r.C: Beriberi is caused by a deficiency of vitamin B1 (thiamine), which is required for PDH, alpha-KGDH, and transketolase.
r.D: Ariboflavinosis is caused by a deficiency of vitamin B2 (riboflavin), which is a precursor to FAD in the TCA cycle.
r.E: Hair loss and dermatitis from raw egg white consumption are associated with deficiency of vitamin B7 (biotin), which is involved in fatty acid, amino acid, and carbohydrate metabolism.

q.s: Slide 8: B Vitamin Overview (SLO 1)

q.v: A researcher is investigating the regulation of glycogen metabolism in isolated hepatocytes following hormonal stimulation. She isolates the enzyme responsible for terminating the intracellular second-messenger cascade by converting cyclic AMP (cAMP) into 5'-AMP. Based on the specific chemical mechanism required to cleave the phosphodiester bond in this reaction, to which of the following enzyme classifications does cyclic AMP phosphodiesterase belong?
o: Kinase
Phosphorylase
Hydrolase
Dehydrogenase
Synthetase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the reaction catalyzed by cyclic AMP phosphodiesterase, which converts cyclic AMP + H2O into 5'-AMP) -> Step 2 (Classify the enzyme as a hydrolase because it catalyzes the addition of H2O to cleave a chemical bond).

r.A: Kinases catalyze the transfer of a phosphate group from a high-energy molecule like ATP to a substrate.
r.B: Phosphorylases add an inorganic phosphate group onto a substrate without utilizing ATP or GTP.
r.D: Dehydrogenases catalyze oxidation-reduction reactions involving the transfer of electrons while removing hydrogen.
r.E: Synthetases join two molecules together using a source of energy such as ATP.

q.s: Slide 15: Hydrolases - Cyclic AMP Phosphodiesterase (SLO 2)

q.v: During an experiment on cellular defense mechanisms against oxidative stress, a molecular biologist isolates an enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of two superoxide radicals (O2-) and two hydrogen ions (2H+) into hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and molecular oxygen (O2). Structural X-ray crystallography of this enzyme's active site reveals multiple histidine and aspartate side chains coordinating two distinct metal cofactor atoms. Which of the following pairs of metal atoms is required for the catalytic activity of this protective enzyme?
o: Iron and molybdenum
Copper and zinc
Magnesium and calcium
Cobalt and selenium
Sulfur and iron
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the enzyme converting 2 O2- + 2H+ to H2O2 + O2 as superoxide dismutase, which protects cells from reactive oxygen) -> Step 2 (Identify the specific metal cofactors coordinated by histidine and aspartate in its active site as copper and zinc [CuZn Superoxide Dismutase]).

r.A: Iron and molybdenum are metal cofactors used by other enzymes, not the cytoplasmic superoxide dismutase shown.
r.C: Magnesium and calcium serve as metal cofactors in various enzymes, but they do not form the active site of CuZn superoxide dismutase.
r.D: Cobalt and selenium are trace metal cofactors, whereas this superoxide dismutase specifically utilizes copper and zinc.
r.E: Iron-sulfur (Fe-S) clusters are found in Complex I (Type 1 NADH Dehydrogenase) of the electron transport chain, not CuZn superoxide dismutase.

q.s: Slide 18: Protection from Reactive Oxygen: CuZn Superoxide Dismutase (SLO 2)

q.v: A pharmacology research team is evaluating a novel neurotoxin that binds to a site distinct from the catalytic active site on a key neurotransmitter-degrading enzyme. In the presence of this toxin, the substrate can still bind to the active site simultaneously, but the resulting physical distortion of the enzyme slows the rate of product formation. When plotting the reaction velocity against substrate concentration, how will the addition of this toxin alter the kinetic parameters compared to an uninhibited control?
o: Decreased apparent Vmax and unchanged Km
Unchanged Vmax and increased apparent Km
Increased apparent Vmax and decreased Km
Decreased apparent Vmax and increased apparent Km
Unchanged Vmax and decreased apparent Km
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the toxin's mechanism as non-competitive inhibition, where the inhibitor binds an allosteric inhibitor site simultaneously with the substrate, distorting the enzyme) -> Step 2 (Determine the kinetic impact of non-competitive inhibition: it decreases the apparent Vmax while leaving the Km unchanged).

r.B: An unchanged Vmax with an increased apparent Km is the classic kinetic profile of a reversible competitive inhibitor.
r.C: Inhibitors decrease reaction rates and do not increase the apparent Vmax of an enzyme.
r.D: Non-competitive inhibitors do not alter the affinity of the unaffected active sites for the substrate, so Km remains unchanged.
r.E: Decreasing the Km would indicate an increase in substrate affinity, whereas non-competitive inhibition leaves Km unchanged and reduces Vmax.

q.s: Slide 25: Non-Competitive Inhibition (SLO 3)

q.v: An investigator is characterizing a newly discovered regulatory enzyme involved in a central metabolic pathway. Structural analysis reveals that the enzyme is multimeric and possesses multiple substrate-binding sites per enzyme molecule. When a specific metabolic effector binds to the enzyme, its quaternary structure is altered, shifting the sigmoidal velocity-versus-substrate curve to the left so that half-maximal velocity is achieved at a much lower substrate concentration without altering Vmax. Which of the following best describes the role of this effector molecule?
o: Competitive antagonist
Irreversible covalent modifier
Positive heterotropic allosteric effector
Negative heterotropic allosteric effector
Zymogen proteolytic activator
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize the multimeric enzyme with a sigmoidal curve and multiple binding sites as an allosteric enzyme) -> Step 2 (Identify that an effector shifting the curve to the left—lowering K0.5/Km and increasing reaction rate at low substrate concentrations—is a positive heterotropic allosteric effector).

r.A: A competitive antagonist binds to the active site and increases the apparent Km, shifting the curve to the right.
r.B: Irreversible covalent modifiers permanently inactivate or activate enzymes via covalent bonds rather than reversible allosteric binding.
r.D: A negative heterotropic allosteric effector shifts the sigmoidal curve to the right, increasing Km and decreasing the reaction rate.
r.E: Zymogen activation involves irreversible proteolytic cleavage of a polypeptide backbone rather than reversible effector binding to a multimeric allosteric enzyme.

q.s: Slides 26-27: Allosteric Enzymes: Heterotropic Effects (SLO 3)

q.v: A 24-year-old man is fasting for 24 hours prior to a scheduled medical procedure. To maintain euglycemia, his pancreatic alpha cells secrete glucagon, which binds to hepatocyte receptors and activates protein kinase A (PKA). In addition to immediately phosphorylating cytoplasmic enzymes to mobilize glycogen, active PKA translocates to the nucleus to regulate gene expression. Which of the following proteins is directly phosphorylated and activated by PKA in the nucleus to increase the transcription of gluconeogenic enzymes and glucose transporters?
o: Cyclic AMP phosphodiesterase
CREB (cyclic AMP response element binding protein)
Phosphorylase kinase
Glycogen synthase
Chymotrypsinogen
q.p: Step 1 (Follow the glucagon -> cAMP -> active PKA signaling pathway into the nucleus during fasting) -> Step 2 (Identify that nuclear PKA phosphorylates and activates the transcription factor CREB, which binds DNA to increase mRNA expression of glucose transporters and gluconeogenic enzymes).

r.A: Cyclic AMP phosphodiesterase is a hydrolase that degrades cAMP to 5'-AMP in the cytoplasm, rather than a nuclear transcription factor.
r.C: Phosphorylase kinase is a cytoplasmic enzyme phosphorylated by PKA to activate glycogen phosphorylase during glycogenolysis.
r.D: Glycogen synthase is a cytoplasmic enzyme that is phosphorylated and inactivated by PKA to halt glycogenesis.
r.E: Chymotrypsinogen is an inactive pancreatic zymogen cleaved in the small intestine to digest dietary proteins.

q.s: Slide 41: Regulation by Gene Expression (SLO 4)

q.v: A molecular biochemist is studying the mechanism of reversible covalent modification on a metabolic enzyme triggered by epinephrine signaling. Using site-directed mutagenesis, she mutates a specific hydroxyl-containing amino acid residue on the target enzyme, which completely prevents protein kinase A (PKA) from phosphorylating the protein. In the native, unmutated enzyme, how does the addition of a negatively charged phosphate group to this specific amino acid residue physically alter the enzyme's activity?
o: It permanently cleaves the polypeptide backbone to expose the active site
It provides chemical groups not found on standard amino acids to directly bind CO2
It disrupts internal electrostatic bonds, leading to a conformational change in the protein
It removes shielding water molecules from the substrate ground state
It joins two separate enzyme subunits together using GTP as an energy source
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the process as reversible serine phosphorylation by a protein kinase) -> Step 2 (Determine the physical mechanism: adding a negatively charged phosphate group to serine disrupts existing electrostatic bonds [between + and - charges] within the protein, causing a conformational change that alters function).

r.A: Permanent cleavage of the polypeptide backbone describes irreversible zymogen activation, such as pepsinogen converting to pepsin.
r.B: Providing chemical groups to transfer CO2 describes the noncovalent coenzyme role of biotin in carboxylase reactions.
r.D: Removing shielding water (desolvation) is how an active site lowers the transition state energy of a substrate, not how phosphorylation alters protein conformation.
r.E: Phosphorylation uses ATP to add a phosphate group to a single polypeptide chain to alter electrostatic interactions, rather than ligating subunits with GTP.

q.s: Slide 39: Closer Look at the Site of Protein Phosphorylation (SLO 4)

q.v: A geneticist is comparing two distinct enzymes isolated from different human tissues that both catalyze the exact same phosphorylation of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate. Sequencing reveals that the two enzymes have different amino acid sequences and are encoded at different genetic loci. Furthermore, they exhibit different electrophoretic mobilities and distinct Km values that refine glucose metabolism for the specific demands of their respective tissues. Which of the following terms best classifies the relationship between these two enzymes?
o: Zymogens
Coenzymes
Isozymes
Transcription factors
Allosteric effectors
q.p: Step 1 (Analyze the properties of the two enzymes: different amino acid sequences, encoded at different genetic loci, different electrophoretic mobilities and Km values, but catalyzing the exact same biochemical reaction) -> Step 2 (Classify this group of enzymes as isozymes).

r.A: Zymogens are inactive enzyme precursors that require irreversible proteolytic cleavage to become active proteases.
r.B: Coenzymes are small organic molecules, such as B vitamins, that bind to enzymes to provide chemical groups not found on amino acid side chains.
r.D: Transcription factors, such as CREB, are regulatory proteins that bind DNA to alter gene expression rather than catalyzing metabolic reactions.
r.E: Allosteric effectors are small molecules like AMP or ATP that bind to multimeric enzymes to alter their catalytic rate.

q.s: Slide 43: Isozymes (SLO 5)

q.v: A 45-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with severe epigastric pain radiating to her back and persistent vomiting. The attending physician suspects acute organ damage and orders a comprehensive serum enzyme panel to localize the tissue injury. While elevated serum alanine transaminase (ALT) would point toward liver damage and elevated CK-BB would indicate brain or smooth muscle injury, a marked elevation in which of the following serum enzyme pairs would most specifically confirm damage to the pancreas?
o: Creatine phosphokinase (CK-MM) and lactate dehydrogenase
Pancreatic lipase and pancreatic amylase
Cardiac troponin and CK-MB
Pepsinogen and glucose-6-phosphatase
Pyruvate dehydrogenase and transketolase
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that organ disease/damage causes tissue-specific intracellular enzymes to leak into the blood for clinical diagnosis) -> Step 2 (Identify pancreatic lipase and pancreatic amylase as the specific serum markers used to diagnose pancreatic damage).

r.A: CK-MM is specific for skeletal muscle damage, and lactate dehydrogenase is a marker used alongside CPK and troponin for cardiac/muscle injury.
r.C: Cardiac troponin and the CK-MB isozyme are specific diagnostic markers for myocardial infarction (heart muscle damage).
r.D: Pepsinogen is secreted by gastric chief cells into the stomach lumen, and glucose-6-phosphatase is an intracellular gluconeogenic enzyme, neither of which is the standard serum pair for pancreatic injury.
r.E: Pyruvate dehydrogenase and transketolase are intracellular vitamin B1-dependent enzymes, not the serum diagnostic markers for pancreatic damage.

q.s: Slides 44-45: Enzymes And Isozymes in Clinical Diagnosis (SLO 5)

q.v: A molecular genetics laboratory is analyzing a newly discovered single-stranded nucleic acid polymer isolated from a human tissue sample. Chemical degradation of the polymer reveals that it is composed of ribose sugars linked to adenine, guanine, cytosine, and a nitrogenous base that lacks a methyl group on its single pyrimidine ring. Before this molecule can be incorporated as a monomer into the polymer chain, it must first be converted from a nucleoside into a nucleotide. Which of the following chemical modifications is directly required to achieve this conversion?
o: Formation of an N-glycosidic bond at the 1' carbon of the sugar
Addition of one to three phosphate groups to the 5' carbon of the sugar
Deoxygenation of the hydroxyl group at the 2' carbon of the sugar
Addition of a methyl group to the single-ring nitrogenous base
Formation of a covalent bond between the 3' carbon and an adjacent nitrogenous base
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the monomer precursor as a ribonucleoside containing uracil, a single-ring pyrimidine without a methyl group, linked to ribose) -> Step 2 (Determine that converting a nucleoside into a nucleotide requires adding 1, 2, or 3 phosphate groups to the 5' carbon position of the sugar).

r.A: An N-glycosidic bond links the nitrogenous base to the 1' carbon of the 5-carbon sugar to form the nucleoside itself, not the conversion of a nucleoside to a nucleotide.
r.C: Removing the oxygen from the 2' hydroxyl group converts ribose into 2'-deoxyribose for DNA synthesis, rather than converting a nucleoside into a nucleotide.
r.D: Adding a methyl group to uracil forms thymine, which is a base modification distinguishing DNA from RNA rather than the phosphorylation step that defines a nucleotide.
r.E: Nucleotides are linked to one another via 5' to 3' phosphodiester bonds between sugars, not by linking the 3' carbon directly to an adjacent nitrogenous base.

q.s: Slide 6 (Nitrogenous Bases), Slide 7 (Nucleoside), and Slide 8 (Nucleotide)

q.v: A researcher is studying a cellular pathway that regulates the expression of specific target genes without altering the underlying genomic DNA sequence. She isolates a class of nucleic acid molecules that contain uracil and ribose sugars, but she observes that these molecules never associate with ribosomes and are never translated into amino acid chains. In the context of the Central Dogma and nucleic acid function, what is the primary role of this specific class of isolated molecules?
o: Serving as the direct template for reverse transcription into protein
Storing the genetic code for transmission from parent to daughter cells
Acting as the primary mRNA intermediary between genomic DNA and polypeptides
Regulating gene expression as non-coding RNAs
Forming the double-stranded B-form helix with major and minor grooves
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the isolated molecule as a ribonucleic acid [RNA] that is not translated into protein, meaning it is a non-coding RNA rather than mRNA) -> Step 2 (Connect non-coding RNAs to their specific cellular function taught in the lecture, which is the regulation of gene expression).

r.A: Reverse transcription synthesizes complementary DNA (cDNA) from an mRNA template, not protein.
r.B: Storing the genetic code and transmitting it to daughter cells and across generations is the defining function of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), not RNA.
r.C: Messenger RNA (mRNA) acts as the translated intermediary between DNA and proteins, whereas the isolated molecule never associates with ribosomes for translation.
r.E: The B-form double-helix with major and minor grooves is the secondary structure of cellular DNA, whereas the isolated molecule is a single-stranded RNA.

q.s: Slide 3 (Nucleic Acids) and Slide 4 (The Central Dogma)

q.v: A 26-year-old man presents to the clinic with painful vesicular lesions on his lips. He is prescribed acyclovir (Zovirax) for a suspected herpes simplex virus infection. Inside the infected cells, the medication is converted into a tri-phosphorylated analog that exhibits a high affinity for the viral polymerase and is incorporated into the growing viral DNA chain, halting replication. Structurally, this therapeutic agent is an analog of a cellular nucleoside that contains which of the following nitrogenous bases?
o: A single-ring pyrimidine containing a methyl group
A two-ring purine that forms three hydrogen bonds with cytosine
A two-ring purine that pairs with thymine via two hydrogen bonds
A single-ring pyrimidine found exclusively in RNA
A single-ring pyrimidine that pairs with guanine
q.p: Step 1 (Identify acyclovir [acycloguanosine] as a guanosine analog missing most of its deoxyribose sugar) -> Step 2 (Determine the structural properties of the guanine base in guanosine: it is a two-ring purine that forms three hydrogen bonds with cytosine in Watson-Crick base pairing).

r.A: A single-ring pyrimidine containing a methyl group describes thymine, which is the base component of azidothymidine (AZT), not acyclovir.
r.C: Adenine is the two-ring purine that pairs with thymine via two hydrogen bonds, whereas acyclovir is an analog of guanosine.
r.D: Uracil is the single-ring pyrimidine found in RNA in place of thymine, which is not the base used in acyclovir.
r.E: Cytosine is a single-ring pyrimidine that pairs with guanine, whereas acyclovir is derived from the purine guanosine.

q.s: Slide 6 (Nitrogenous Bases), Slide 12 (Clinical correlation: Nucleoside analogs - Acyclovir), and Slide 18 (Secondary Structure of DNA)

q.v: A 19-year-old woman with a history of recurrent sinopulmonary infections and thick, sticky mucus buildup in her lungs is treated with inhaled recombinant human DNase (dornase alpha) to clear her airways. In the laboratory, a biochemist compares the enzymatic activity of this therapeutic DNase against a strictly 3'-specific exonuclease using a linear double-stranded DNA fragment with the single-strand sequence 5'-dACGT-3' released from dying white blood cells. Unlike the 3'-specific exonuclease, the enzyme used to treat this patient's condition is capable of directly hydrolyzing which of the following bonds?
o: The N-glycosidic bond linking the thymine base to its 2'-deoxyribose sugar
The internal phosphodiester bond between the cytosine and guanine nucleotides
The hydrogen bonds between complementary adenine and thymine bases
The covalent bond attaching the 5' phosphate group to the 5' carbon of deoxyadenosine
The terminal phosphodiester bond exclusively at the 3' hydroxyl end of the chain
q.p: Step 1 (Identify recombinant human DNase used in cystic fibrosis as a nuclease that cleaves extracellular DNA, and distinguish endonucleases from exonucleases) -> Step 2 (Recognize that while a 3'-exonuclease only cleaves from the 3' end of the DNA, an endonuclease cleaves internal 5'-to-3' phosphodiester bonds, such as the one between internal cytosine and guanine nucleotides in 5'-dACGT-3').

r.A: Nucleases cleave polynucleotide chains by hydrolyzing phosphodiester bonds in the sugar-phosphate backbone, not the N-glycosidic bonds between the sugar and nitrogenous base.
r.C: Hydrogen bonds stabilize base pairing between antiparallel strands in the secondary double-helix structure, whereas nucleases hydrolyze covalent phosphodiester bonds of the primary structure.
r.D: Nucleases hydrolyze the 3'-5' phosphodiester bridges linking adjacent nucleotides rather than stripping the terminal 5' monophosphate from the 5' carbon of the first sugar.
r.E: Cleaving strictly from the 3' end of the DNA polynucleotide chain is the specific mechanism of a 3' exonuclease, not an internal-cleaving endonuclease.

q.s: Slide 14 (Primary structure of DNA), Slide 15 (Nucleases), and Slide 16 (Clinical correlation: DNase treatment for cystic fibrosis)

q.v: A molecular biologist is investigating a newly identified genetic disorder characterized by severely reduced protein levels of a vital metabolic enzyme, despite normal rates of transcription initiation by RNA polymerase. Sequencing of the patient's gene reveals intact TATA and CAAT boxes, normal enhancer regions, and unaltered coding sequences within the exons. However, a point mutation is discovered within the 3' untranslated region (3' UTR) that abolishes the consensus sequence 5'-AAUAAA-3' in the RNA transcript. Which of the following downstream molecular defects is the most likely consequence of this mutation?
o: Inability of the mature mRNA to bind to the ribosome to initiate translation
Failure of transcription factors to bind the promoter and initiate RNA synthesis
Impaired mRNA stability due to loss of the poly-A binding/polyadenylation signal
Inclusion of intervening intron sequences into the final translated peptide
Premature termination of translation at the ATG start codon
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the 5'-AAUAAA-3' [AATAAA in DNA] sequence in the 3' UTR as the polyadenylation signal / poly-A binding sequence) -> Step 2 (Deduce that disrupting the 3' UTR poly-A sequence impairs the addition of the poly-A tail, which normally regulates mRNA stability).

r.A: Binding to the ribosome to initiate translation is the specific function of the 5' untranslated region (5' UTR), not the 3' UTR.
r.B: Transcription factors and RNA polymerase bind to the promoter (containing TATA and CAAT boxes) to initiate transcription, which is intact in this patient.
r.D: Removal of intervening sequences (introns) occurs during pre-mRNA splicing mediated by GT/AG (GU/AG) splice sites, not the 3' UTR polyadenylation signal.
r.E: The ATG codon in the first exon serves as the translation start site, whereas the Stop codon terminates translation upstream of the 3' UTR.

q.s: Slide 19 (Anatomy of a Gene), Slide 20 (Anatomy of a Gene and the Central Dogma), and Slide 21-22 (Anatomy of a Gene - First Aid)

q.v: A 16-year-old boy is evaluated for progressive difficulty walking and frequent stumbling (ataxia). Genetic testing confirms an autosomal recessive disorder caused by an unstable trinucleotide repeat expansion of (GAA)n to over 70 copies. In contrast to the genetic mutation responsible for Huntington disease, where is the expanded trinucleotide repeat located within the affected gene of this 16-year-old patient, and what is its direct molecular consequence?
o: Located in the promoter/5' UTR, resulting in promoter methylation and gene silencing
Located in an exon, resulting in an expanded polyglutamine tract in the protein
Located in the 3' UTR, resulting in the production of toxic RNA transcripts
Located in an intron, resulting in reduced gene expression
Located in an enhancer, resulting in increased transcriptional efficiency
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the patient's autosomal recessive ataxia with a >70 GAA repeat expansion as Friedreich ataxia) -> Step 2 (Map the GAA expansion in Friedreich ataxia to an intron within the gene, which directly leads to reduced gene expression, contrasting with the exonic CAG repeat in Huntington disease).

r.A: A CGG repeat expansion in the 5' UTR/promoter causing promoter methylation and gene silencing is the mechanism of Fragile X syndrome, an X-linked dominant disorder.
r.B: A CAG repeat expansion within an exon leading to protein polyglutamination is the mechanism of autosomal dominant Huntington disease.
r.C: A CTG repeat expansion in the 3' UTR of the DMPK gene producing toxic RNA is the mechanism of autosomal dominant Myotonic dystrophy type 1.
r.E: Enhancers bind specific transcription factors to regulate transcriptional efficiency, and none of the four classic trinucleotide repeat diseases taught involve enhancer expansions.

q.s: Slide 25 (Trinucleotide Repeat Expansion Diseases), Slide 26 (Trinucleotide repeat expansion location within the gene), and Slide 27 (Trinucleotide Repeat Expansion Diseases diagram)

q.v: A 42-year-old man is evaluated for progressive involuntary movements, emotional disturbances, and cognitive decline. His father developed similar neurological symptoms at age 62, whereas the patient's 18-year-old son was recently diagnosed with severe juvenile-onset symptoms of the same autosomal dominant condition. The molecular mechanism driving the generational increase in repeat numbers in this family involves temporary dissociation of the newly synthesized DNA strand from the template strand during replication. For the newly synthesized DNA strand to become longer than the original template strand, which of the following structural events must occur during replication?
o: Formation of a hairpin loop within the template strand, bypassing repeat units
Formation of a loop within the newly synthesized strand, allowing re-replication of template repeats
Cleavage of both DNA strands by Topoisomerase II followed by impaired religation
Substitution of thymine with uracil in the coding exon during strand elongation
Hydrolysis of internal phosphodiester bonds by cellular endonucleases
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the family's clinical presentation and earlier age of onset in successive generations as genetic anticipation in Huntington disease, driven by trinucleotide repeat expansion via DNA strand slippage) -> Step 2 (Distinguish expansion from contraction in DNA strand slippage: expansion [new strand longer than original] occurs when the newly synthesized 5'-to-3' strand dissociates and forms a loop out of the repeat region, whereas looping of the template strand causes contraction).

r.A: When the template strand forms a loop during strand dissociation, the polymerase skips the looped template repeat, resulting in contraction where the new strand is shorter than the original.
r.C: Double-stranded DNA cleavage and rejoining is the mechanism of Topoisomerase II to alter tertiary supercoiling, not the mechanism of trinucleotide repeat expansion.
r.D: Huntington disease is caused by an unstable CAG triplet repeat expansion in an exon encoding glutamine, not by uracil misincorporation.
r.E: Endonuclease cleavage of internal phosphodiester bonds fragments DNA chains rather than elongating repeat regions during replication.

q.s: Slide 28 (Characteristics of Trinucleotide Repeat Expansion Diseases), Slide 29 (Genetic Anticipation in Huntington's Disease), Slide 31 (DNA Strand Slippage - Expansion), and Slide 32 (DNA Strand Slippage - Contraction)

q.v: A 58-year-old man undergoing chemotherapy for metastatic cancer receives irinotecan, a derivative of a compound originally extracted from the bark of the Camptotheca acuminata tree. The patient is concurrently taking ciprofloxacin for a bacterial urinary tract infection. Although both medications target enzymes that regulate the tertiary supercoiled structure of DNA by introducing swivel points, irinotecan causes toxicity in rapidly dividing human cells while ciprofloxacin selectively inhibits bacterial DNA synthesis without affecting host cells. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of action of irinotecan compared to ciprofloxacin?
o: Irinotecan blocks ATP hydrolysis required by human topoisomerases to rejoin broken DNA strands
Irinotecan targets human Topoisomerase I by cutting a single DNA strand and inhibiting its religation
Irinotecan inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase by preventing the introduction of negative supercoils
Irinotecan cleaves both strands of the eukaryotic DNA double-helix via Topoisomerase II inhibition
Irinotecan acts as a guanosine analog that terminates elongation of the supercoiled DNA helix
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize irinotecan/topotecan as camptothecin [CPT] derivatives used in chemotherapy, and ciprofloxacin as a quinolone targeting bacterial-specific Topoisomerase II / DNA gyrase) -> Step 2 (Identify that camptothecin derivatives target Topoisomerase I, which cuts a single strand of the DNA double-helix, and specifically inhibit the reformation/religation of the cleaved DNA, leading to cell toxicity during DNA replication).

r.A: According to the lecture materials, topoisomerases break DNA strands, pass the strand(s) through the break, and rejoin them without using ATP.
r.C: Blocking DNA gyrase (a bacterial-specific topoisomerase II that introduces negative supercoils and relieves positive supercoils) is the mechanism of quinolone drugs like ciprofloxacin and nalidixic acid.
r.D: Topoisomerase II cuts both strands of the double-helix, whereas camptothecin derivatives like irinotecan specifically target Topoisomerase I, which cuts only a single strand.
r.E: Acting as a guanosine analog that cannot be extended is the mechanism of acyclovir in treating herpes simplex virus, not the topoisomerase inhibitor irinotecan.

q.s: Slide 34-35 (DNA Topoisomerases) and Slide 36-37 (Clinical correlation: Topoisomerase inhibitors)

q.v: An electron microscopy study is conducted to visualize the hierarchical packaging of double-stranded human DNA into a nucleus that measures approximately 6 micrometers in diameter. The researcher treats isolated mitotic chromosomes with a mild salt solution to dissociate scaffolding proteins and unfold the 30-nm chromatin solenoids into 10-nm nucleofilaments ('beads on a string'). She then isolates a single 'bead' (the nucleosome core particle) after digesting away the linker DNA and Histone H1. Chemical analysis of this isolated nucleosome core particle will reveal approximately 146 base pairs of DNA wrapped 1.75 turns around an octamer composed of which of the following protein subunits?
o: Eight copies of Histone H1
One copy each of H1, H2A, H2B, and H3
Two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4
Four copies each of H3 and H4 only
Two copies each of H1, H2A, H2B, and H4
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the isolated 146 bp, 1.75-turn particle without H1 as the nucleosome core, the basic unit of chromatin making up the 10-nm nucleofilament) -> Step 2 (Determine the exact composition of the histone octamer at the center of the nucleosome core: two copies of each core histone H2A, H2B, H3, and H4).

r.A: Histone H1 is the linker histone that binds outside the nucleosome core to form a 166 bp, two-turn chromatosome, and does not form the core octamer.
r.B: An octamer requires eight total histone subunits (two copies of four core histones), and H1 is excluded from the nucleosome core particle.
r.D: While H3 and H4 are part of the core, the histone octamer requires two copies each of H2A and H2B in addition to two copies each of H3 and H4.
r.E: Histone H1 is the linker histone rather than a core histone, and Histone H3 is missing from this combination.

q.s: Slide 38-39 (Chromosome Structure / From DNA to Chromosome), Slide 40 (Nucleosome: the Basic Unit of Chromatin), and Slide 41 (Chromatosome)

q.v: A researcher is investigating how post-translational modifications of chromatin regulate gene transcription in eukaryotic cells. She focuses on the flexible, protruding segments of core histone proteins that do not form the globular center of the nucleosome octamer, but instead extend outward to interact with DNA, regulatory proteins, and histones in adjacent nucleosomes. Which of the following specific structural domains of the core histones is the researcher studying?
o: The negatively charged C-terminal domains rich in aspartate and glutamate
The N-terminal tails of the core histones
The 3' untranslated poly-A binding tails
The major and minor grooves of the B-form histone helix
The central scaffolding protein loops of the 700-nm condensed chromosome
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the protruding histone segments that undergo post-translational modifications to regulate gene expression and interact with adjacent nucleosomes) -> Step 2 (Pinpoint these domains from the lecture as the N-terminal tails of the histones).

r.A: Histones are cationic (positively charged) proteins with an unusually high content of basic amino acids (arginine, lysine, and histidine), not negatively charged acidic domains.
r.C: The 3' UTR and poly-A tail are structural features of messenger RNA (mRNA) transcripts that regulate mRNA stability, not protein domains of histones.
r.D: Major and minor grooves are structural features of the B-form DNA double-helix secondary structure, not of histone proteins.
r.E: Scaffolding proteins attach to looped 30-nm solenoids to form higher-order chromosome structures (300-nm to 700-nm), whereas the N-terminal tails are part of the core histones within the nucleosome.

q.s: Slide 39 (From DNA to Chromosome), Slide 40 (Nucleosome diagram showing N-tails), and Slide 42 (Histones)

q.v: A researcher is characterizing the biochemical structure of a monomer isolated from a genomic DNA library. Mass spectrometry confirms the molecule is a pyrimidine nucleotide that contains a methyl group attached to its nitrogenous ring. In its nucleoside form prior to phosphorylation, which of the following bonds directly links this specific nitrogenous base to the 1' carbon of the 2'-deoxyribose sugar?
o: 3'-5' phosphodiester bond
N-glycosidic bond
Two Watson-Crick hydrogen bonds
Three Watson-Crick hydrogen bonds
Peptide bond
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the monomer as deoxythymidine monophosphate based on the methylated pyrimidine ring and 2'-deoxyribose sugar) -> Step 2 (Recognize that a nucleoside consists of a nitrogenous base linked to a 5-carbon sugar at the 1' position via an N-glycosidic bond).

r.A: A 3'-5' phosphodiester bond links adjacent nucleotides together to form the sugar-phosphate polynucleotide backbone rather than attaching the base to the sugar.
r.C: Two hydrogen bonds form between complementary adenine and thymine bases on opposite antiparallel DNA strands rather than linking a base to its own sugar.
r.D: Three hydrogen bonds form between complementary cytosine and guanine bases in double-stranded DNA.
r.E: Peptide bonds link amino acids together in the primary structure of proteins, not nucleic acids.

q.s: Slide 6 (Nitrogenous Bases) and Slide 7 (Nucleoside)

q.v: A 45-year-old man is being evaluated for a Newly diagnosed viral infection. Laboratory analysis of the viral replication cycle reveals that the pathogen is an RNA-containing virus that synthesizes complementary DNA (cDNA) from its viral mRNA template inside host cells. If a nucleoside analog lacking a 3' hydroxyl group is administered to inhibit this specific viral enzyme, which of the following host cellular enzymes is spared due to its much lower affinity for the phosphorylated drug?
o: Exonuclease
Endonuclease
DNA polymerase
RNA polymerase
Bacterial DNA gyrase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the viral process as reverse transcription in HIV and the drug as Azidothymidine [AZT]) -> Step 2 (Conclude that viral reverse transcriptase has a much higher affinity for AZT than host DNA polymerase, minimizing negative cellular consequences).

r.A: Exonucleases cleave nucleotides from the 5' or 3' ends of DNA chains rather than synthesizing DNA polymers.
r.B: Endonucleases cleave internal phosphodiester bonds within polynucleotide chains and are not the primary off-target polymerizing enzyme spared by AZT's selectivity.
r.D: RNA polymerase catalyzes transcription of genomic DNA into mRNA and does not incorporate deoxythymidine analogs like AZT.
r.E: DNA gyrase is a bacterial-specific topoisomerase II targeted by quinolones, which is entirely absent in eukaryotic host cells.

q.s: Slide 4 (The Central Dogma) and Slide 11 (Clinical correlation: Nucleoside analogs - AZT)

q.v: A molecular geneticist is analyzing a single-stranded fragment of human genomic DNA that was generated by treatment with a specific nuclease. Sequencing of the isolated oligonucleotide reveals the directional sequence 5'-dACGT-3'. If the researcher treats this fragment with an enzyme that specifically hydrolyzes the terminal nucleotide containing a free hydroxyl group on its sugar ring, which of the following nitrogenous bases will be released first?
o: Adenine
Cytosine
Guanine
Thymine
Uracil
q.p: Step 1 (Determine that DNA sequences are written directionally from the 5' phosphate end to the 3' OH end, making Thymine the terminal nucleotide with a free 3' OH group in 5'-dACGT-3') -> Step 2 (Apply the mechanism of a 3'-specific exonuclease, which cleaves from the 3' end of the DNA to release the thymine-containing nucleotide first).

r.A: Adenine is located at the 5' end of the 5'-dACGT-3' sequence, which possesses a free 5' phosphate group rather than a 3' hydroxyl group.
r.B: Cytosine is located at an internal position within the polynucleotide chain, which would require an endonuclease rather than an exonuclease for cleavage.
r.C: Guanine is located at an internal position within the oligonucleotide and does not have a free 3' hydroxyl group.
r.E: Uracil is a pyrimidine base found in RNA in place of thymine and is absent from this deoxyribonucleotide sequence.

q.s: Slide 14 (Primary structure of DNA) and Slide 15 (Nucleases)

q.v: A biochemist is studying the three-dimensional structural hierarchy of nucleic acids and proteins in human cells. She isolates a native, relaxed genomic DNA molecule in its most common physiological secondary structure, which features distinct major and minor grooves. Which of the following protein structural elements represents the equivalent level of structural organization to this double-helical DNA conformation?
o: Amino acid chain
Alpha-helix and beta-strand
Numerous tertiary conformations
Supercoiled helices
Histone octamer complex
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the relaxed B-form DNA double-helix with major and minor grooves as the secondary structure of DNA) -> Step 2 (Match the secondary structure of DNA to the equivalent secondary structure of proteins, which consists of alpha-helices, beta-strands, and turns).

r.A: An amino acid chain represents the primary structure of a protein, which corresponds to the linear polynucleotide chain of DNA.
r.C: Numerous three-dimensional conformations represent the tertiary structure of proteins, which corresponds to supercoiled DNA helices.
r.D: Supercoiled helices represent the tertiary structure of DNA rather than a structural level of proteins.
r.E: The histone octamer is a multiprotein complex involved in chromatin packaging (nucleosomes) rather than the equivalent secondary structure of a single protein.

q.s: Slide 13 (Comparison between protein and DNA structure) and Slide 17 (Secondary Structure of DNA)

q.v: A 6-year-old boy is evaluated for severe anemia caused by defective expression of a critical globin protein. Genetic sequencing of the affected locus reveals a point mutation within the 3' untranslated region (3' UTR) that alters the consensus sequence 5'-AAUAAA-3' in the primary RNA transcript. Disruption of this specific sequence element most likely impairs protein production by interfering with which of the following molecular functions?
o: Binding of transcription factors and RNA polymerase to initiate transcription
Binding of the mature mRNA to the ribosome to initiate translation
Excision of intervening sequences during pre-mRNA splicing
Addition of the poly-A tail that regulates mRNA stability
Encoding the initial methionine amino acid at the translation start site
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the 5'-AAUAAA-3' sequence in the 3' UTR as the polyadenylation signal/poly-A binding sequence) -> Step 2 (Deduce that mutating this region impairs the poly-A tail addition, which likely regulates mRNA stability).

r.A: Transcription factors and RNA polymerase bind to the promoter region (such as TATA and CAAT boxes) upstream of the transcription start site.
r.B: Binding to the ribosome for translation is the primary function of the 5' untranslated region (5' UTR) of the exon.
r.C: Excision of intervening sequences (introns) during splicing relies on splice site signals (such as GT and AG in DNA / GU and AG in pre-mRNA) located between exons.
r.E: The initial methionine (Met) is encoded by the ATG/AUG start codon at the translation start site, not the 3' UTR.

q.s: Slide 19 (Anatomy of a Gene) and Slide 21-22 (Anatomy of a Gene: Central Dogma)

q.v: A 14-year-old boy is brought to the clinic for evaluation of developmental delay. Physical examination reveals a protruding chin and enlarged testes (macro-orchidism). Genetic testing confirms an X-linked dominant disorder caused by an expansion of more than 200 trinucleotide repeats in the 5' untranslated region (UTR) of the affected gene. By which of the following downstream mechanisms does this specific repeat expansion cause disease?
o: Production of a toxic RNA molecule that sequesters splicing proteins
Accumulation of polyglutamine tracts within the translated protein
Promoter methylation leading to transcriptional gene silencing
Impaired pre-mRNA splicing due to an intronic repeat expansion
Frameshift mutation resulting in a premature stop codon
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the clinical presentation of protruding chin, giant gonads, X-linked dominant inheritance, and >200 repeats in the 5' UTR as Fragile X syndrome with a CGG repeat) -> Step 2 (Connect Fragile X syndrome to its specific molecular pathogenesis: promoter methylation leading to gene silencing).

r.A: Production of toxic RNA from a 3' UTR (CTG)n expansion is the mechanism of Myotonic dystrophy type 1.
r.B: Protein polyglutamination results from an exonic (CAG)n repeat expansion in Huntington disease.
r.D: Intronic (GAA)n repeat expansion causing reduced gene expression is the mechanism of Friedreich ataxia.
r.E: Trinucleotide repeat expansions involve multiples of three nucleotides and cause disease via methylation, toxic RNA, or polyglutamination rather than simple frameshift premature stop codons.

q.s: Slide 25-27 (Trinucleotide Repeat Expansion Diseases and Location Within the Gene)

q.v: A 28-year-old woman presents with difficulty releasing her hand after a handshake, muscle pain, and cardiac arrhythmias. Genetic testing of her family reveals that her grandfather had cataracts removed in his 60s with 45 copies of a (CTG)n repeat in the DMPK gene, whereas the patient has 450 copies and her newborn son has 1,500 copies with severe congenital disease. Which of the following molecular events during DNA replication directly accounts for the generation of a longer DNA strand in the offspring?
o: Dissociation of the newly synthesized strand followed by formation of a hairpin loop in the template strand
Dissociation of the newly synthesized strand followed by loop-out formation within the newly synthesized strand
Double-stranded DNA breaks induced by excessive positive supercoiling ahead of the replication fork
Failure of exonucleolytic proofreading to excise mismatched purine-pyrimidine base pairs
Hydrolysis of internal phosphodiester bonds within the 3' UTR by endogenous endonucleases
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize the clinical scenario as genetic anticipation in Myotonic Dystrophy caused by expansion of an unstable CTG repeat from premutation/mild range to full mutation) -> Step 2 (Identify the mechanism of repeat expansion via DNA strand slippage: during replication, strand dissociation occurs and the newly synthesized 5'->3' strand loops out, resulting in a new strand that is longer than the original).

r.A: When the template strand forms a loop-out during strand slippage, replication produces a new strand that is shorter than the original (contraction).
r.C: Double-stranded DNA breaks related to supercoiling are managed by topoisomerases and do not explain trinucleotide repeat expansion.
r.D: Trinucleotide repeat expansion is driven by DNA strand slippage of repetitive sequences rather than point mismatch proofreading failure.
r.E: Endonuclease cleavage of internal phosphodiester bonds degrades DNA rather than expanding repeat copy numbers during replication.

q.s: Slide 24 (Myotonic Dystrophy) and Slide 30-32 (DNA Strand Slippage)

q.v: A 64-year-old woman with metastatic colon cancer is started on a chemotherapeutic regimen containing topotecan, while concurrently receiving nalidixic acid for an uncomplicated urinary tract infection. Although both medications inhibit enzymes that alter the tertiary structure of DNA by introducing 'swivel points' without using ATP, the urinary tract antibiotic does not cause toxicity in the patient's healthy dividing cells. Which of the following best explains the selective safety of the antibiotic compared to the chemotherapy agent?
o: The antibiotic targets an enzyme that cleaves only a single DNA strand, whereas chemotherapy targets double-strand cleavage
Human cells lack the specific type II topoisomerase that introduces negative supercoils into bacterial DNA
The antibiotic requires activation by a viral kinase that is absent in uninfected human cells
Eukaryotic topoisomerases require ATP hydrolysis to rejoin cleaved DNA strands, rendering them resistant to the antibiotic
The chemotherapy agent selectively binds to the 30-nm chromatin solenoid, which is absent in prokaryotic cells
q.p: Step 1 (Identify topotecan as a camptothecin derivative targeting human topoisomerase I, and nalidixic acid as a quinolone targeting bacterial topoisomerase II / DNA gyrase) -> Step 2 (Conclude that quinolones block DNA gyrase—which introduces negative supercoils and relieves positive supercoils—and eukaryotes do not have gyrase, so human cells are unaffected).

r.A: Topotecan (a camptothecin derivative) targets topoisomerase I, which cuts a single strand of DNA, whereas nalidixic acid targets bacterial topoisomerase II, which cuts both strands.
r.C: Activation by phosphorylation in virus-infected cells describes nucleoside analogs like acyclovir, not quinolone antibiotics.
r.D: As taught in the lecture, topoisomerases break one or both DNA strands, pass the strands through the break, and rejoin them without using ATP.
r.E: Topotecan targets topoisomerase I to impair religation of cleaved single-stranded DNA during replication, rather than binding the 30-nm solenoid.

q.s: Slide 34-37 (DNA Topoisomerases and Clinical Correlation: Topoisomerase Inhibitors)

q.v: A structural biologist is examining the compaction of eukaryotic chromatin using high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy. She isolates an individual repeating core particle composed of a histone octamer wrapped by 1.75 turns of double-stranded DNA. When a specific linker protein is added to this preparation, the DNA wraps into a full two-turn particle containing 166 base pairs of DNA. Which of the following accurately describes the protein composition of the initial 1.75-turn core particle prior to the addition of the linker protein?
o: One copy each of histones H1, H2A, H2B, and H3
Two copies each of histones H1, H2A, H2B, and H4
Two copies each of histones H2A, H2B, H3, and H4
Four copies each of histones H3 and H4
One copy of histone H1 and two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the 1.75-turn particle containing ~146 bp of DNA as the nucleosome core, and the two-turn 166 bp particle with H1 as the chromatosome) -> Step 2 (Determine that the nucleosome core octamer consists of two copies of each core histone: H2A, H2B, H3, and H4).

r.A: The nucleosome core is an octamer containing two copies of four core histones (H2A, H2B, H3, H4), and does not contain the linker histone H1.
r.B: Histone H1 is the linker histone added to form a chromatosome and is not part of the core histone octamer; H3 is present instead.
r.D: The histone octamer requires two copies each of H2A and H2B in addition to two copies each of H3 and H4.
r.E: A nucleosome core plus one copy of histone H1 and an additional 20 bp of DNA (166 bp total) defines the chromatosome, not the initial 1.75-turn nucleosome core.

q.s: Slide 40 (Nucleosome: the Basic Unit of Chromatin) and Slide 41 (Chromatosome)

q.v: A researcher is engineering a synthetic histone octamer to study the physical forces that stabilize the 10-nm 'beads on a string' nucleofilament. In the wild-type protein, the globular core domains form strong electrostatic interactions with the exterior of the DNA double helix. If the researcher mutates the amino acid residues responsible for this electrostatic attraction to neutral alanines, which of the following combinations of wild-type amino acids was most likely replaced, and what is the specific DNA chemical group with which they normally interact?
o: Aspartate, glutamate, and histidine interacting with the positively charged nitrogenous bases
Arginine, lysine, and histidine interacting with the negatively charged phosphodiester backbone
Lysine, leucine, and valine interacting with the uncharged 2'-deoxyribose sugar rings
Arginine, aspartate, and cysteine interacting with the hydrogen bonds of the minor groove
Glutamine, asparagine, and histidine interacting with the 3' hydroxyl termini of the DNA strands
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the electrostatic stabilization of nucleosomes as the interaction between cationic histone proteins and anionic DNA) -> Step 2 (Recall that histones have an unusually high content of basic, cationic amino acids—Arginine, Lysine, and Histidine—which interact directly with the negatively charged phosphodiester backbone of DNA).

r.A: Aspartate and glutamate are acidic (negatively charged) amino acids that would repel DNA, and the negative charge of DNA resides on the phosphate backbone rather than the nitrogenous bases.
r.C: Leucine and valine are hydrophobic amino acids, and the electrostatic interaction occurs with the negatively charged phosphate groups rather than the deoxyribose sugars.
r.D: Aspartate and cysteine are not basic cationic amino acids, and histones wrap DNA via electrostatic attraction to the phosphodiester backbone.
r.E: Glutamine and asparagine are uncharged polar amino acids, and histones bind along the length of the internal phosphodiester backbone rather than only at the 3' OH termini.

q.s: Slide 39 (From DNA to Chromosome) and Slide 42 (Histones)
