q.v: A researcher is studying a tumor biopsy from a 54-year-old male and observes that a specific subpopulation of quiescent tumor cells is able to bypass the G1 restriction point and enter the S phase of the cell cycle. For these cells to successfully progress into mitosis, complete replication of the genome must occur during this S phase. Which of the following best describes the composition of the resulting DNA helices at the conclusion of this phase?
o: One helix composed entirely of parental strands and one helix composed entirely of newly synthesized daughter strands
Two helices in which each individual strand is a random mosaic of alternating parental and daughter DNA segments
Two helices that each contain one intact parental template strand paired with one newly synthesized complementary daughter strand
Two helices composed entirely of newly synthesized daughter strands following the complete degradation of the parental template
Four single-stranded DNA molecules that remain unassociated until chromosome condensation begins in mitosis
q.p: Step 1 (Cells pass the Rb/p53-modulated G1 restriction point to enter the S phase of the cell cycle) -> Step 2 (DNA replication in S phase is semi-conservative, meaning each replicated molecule contains one parental strand and one newly synthesized complementary daughter strand).

r.A: This describes conservative replication, whereas human DNA replication is semi-conservative so that each parental strand serves as a template for a new partner strand.
r.B: This describes dispersive replication, whereas replicated DNA molecules maintain intact parental template strands paired with continuous complementary daughter strands.
r.D: Parental strands are conserved to serve as templates during semi-conservative replication rather than being degraded.
r.E: During S phase, each strand of the double-helix immediately serves as a template to synthesize a paired, anti-parallel complementary daughter strand.

q.s: Slide 3: Cell Cycle & Slide 4: DNA Replication Overview

q.v: A 28-year-old female presents with dysuria and urinary frequency, and a urine culture grows Escherichia coli. In the laboratory, an experimental compound is added to the bacterial culture that prevents initiator proteins from binding to their specific target sites on the bacterial chromosome, completely halting the start of S-phase equivalent DNA synthesis. The specific chromosomal region targeted by this compound normally exhibits which of the following characteristics in E. coli?
o: It is present in thousands of copies scattered throughout a linear chromosome
It is a single genomic region rich in adenine-thymine base pairs that opens to form two bi-directional replication forks
It is a guanine-cytosine-rich terminal loop structure that protects the chromosome ends from degradation
It initiates synthesis unidirectionally using a single replication fork that travels around the circular genome
It requires an intrinsic ribonucleoprotein reverse transcriptase to synthesize the initial template strand
q.p: Step 1 (Initiator proteins bind at the replication origin in prokaryotes like E. coli) -> Step 2 (In E. coli, DNA is replicated from a single origin rich in A:T base pairs where partial opening of the helix establishes bi-directional replication at two replication forks).

r.A: Prokaryotic E. coli DNA is circular and replicated from a single origin, whereas eukaryotic chromosomes are linear and have multiple origins of replication.
r.C: Guanine-rich terminal loop structures (T loops) describe eukaryotic telomeres, not the prokaryotic origin of replication.
r.D: Prokaryotic replication is bi-directional and occurs simultaneously at two replication forks formed at the local opening of the origin.
r.E: A ribonucleoprotein reverse transcriptase describes telomerase at eukaryotic chromosomal ends, whereas prokaryotic initiation relies on initiator proteins opening an A:T-rich double helix.

q.s: Slide 5: Initiation of Replication (Prokaryotes)

q.v: In a biochemical assay modeling bacterial DNA replication, helicase unwinds a double-stranded DNA template in the presence of all four deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) and purified DNA polymerase III. Despite adequate dNTP precursors and an open single-stranded template, no new DNA synthesis occurs until a second enzyme is added that copies a short stretch of the DNA template in the 5' to 3' direction. What specific molecular feature is provided by the product of this second enzyme to allow DNA polymerase III to begin chain elongation?
o: A free 5'-triphosphate group that undergoes hydrolysis to drive template unwinding
A 3'-OH terminus on a short RNA segment that enables nucleophilic attack on incoming dNTPs
A DNA-based sliding clamp that tethers the polymerase to the parental strand
A 3' to 5' exonuclease cleavage site that removes supercoils ahead of the fork
An adenosine triphosphate-activated 5'-phosphate group for immediate nick sealing
q.p: Step 1 (DNA polymerases cannot initiate synthesis de novo from a single-stranded template and require RNA primase to synthesize a short RNA primer) -> Step 2 (The RNA primer provides a free 3'-OH group needed for DNA polymerase to extend the chain via nucleophilic attack on the innermost phosphate of an incoming dNTP).

r.A: Chain elongation is driven by the nucleophilic attack of the primer's 3'-OH terminus on the incoming dNTP, not by a 5'-triphosphate on the primer.
r.C: The second enzyme described is RNA primase (an RNA polymerase), which synthesizes a short RNA primer to provide a 3'-OH rather than a protein sliding clamp.
r.D: 3' to 5' exonuclease activity is a proofreading function of DNA polymerases, whereas RNA primase synthesizes a 5' to 3' RNA primer to initiate synthesis.
r.E: ATP-dependent formation of a phosphodiester bond between a 5'-phosphate and 3'-OH is the mechanism of DNA ligase for sealing nicks, not initiating synthesis.

q.s: Slide 7-10: RNA Priming & Slide 13: Chain Elongation

q.v: A 41-year-old male living with HIV is started on a single-agent antiretroviral regimen targeting the viral RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (reverse transcriptase). Although his viral load initially drops, within several months his plasma HIV RNA levels rebound dramatically, and viral sequencing reveals multiple point mutations conferring drug resistance. Which of the following enzymatic deficiencies in the viral polymerase directly explains the rapid emergence of these resistant mutant viruses?
o: Inability to catalyze the release of pyrophosphate during phosphodiester bond formation
Lack of 5' to 3' exonuclease activity required to excise ribonucleotide primers
Absence of 3' to 5' exonuclease activity to remove non-complementary nucleotides
Failure to utilize deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates as precursors for 5' to 3' synthesis
Inability to assemble into a multi-enzyme replisome complex with host histones
q.p: Step 1 (Rapid emergence of drug-resistant mutant HIV strains during monotherapy) -> Step 2 (HIV reverse transcriptase lacks 3' to 5' proofreading exonuclease activity, resulting in an inability to remove mismatched nucleotides and a much higher error/mutation rate).

r.A: Viral reverse transcriptase is a functional DNA polymerase that successfully forms phosphodiester bonds by releasing pyrophosphate from incoming dNTPs.
r.B: 5' to 3' exonuclease activity is used by bacterial DNA polymerase I to remove RNA primers from Okazaki fragments, not for proofreading newly added bases.
r.D: Reverse transcriptase actively synthesizes DNA in the 5' to 3' direction using dNTPs, which is why nucleoside analogs like AZT can be phosphorylated and incorporated by it.
r.E: The high mutation rate of HIV is directly caused by the absence of 3' to 5' proofreading ability in reverse transcriptase, necessitating combination therapy.

q.s: Slide 12: Proofreading & Slide 15: Clinical correlation (HIV reverse transcriptase)

q.v: A molecular biologist is investigating a temperature-sensitive mutant strain of E. coli. When shifted to a restrictive temperature during the S-phase equivalent, DNA polymerase III successfully synthesizes Okazaki fragments until encountering the downstream RNA primer, and DNA polymerase I successfully excises the RNA primers and fills the resulting gaps with DNA nucleotides. However, alkaline gel electrophoresis reveals that the newly synthesized lagging strand remains broken into short, unjoined DNA segments. The enzyme that is defective in this mutant requires which of the following to complete lagging strand maturation?
o: A ribonucleoprotein RNA template to extend the 3' overhang of the lagging strand
Cleavage of the innermost phosphate of an incoming dNTP with the release of pyrophosphate
3' to 5' exonuclease hydrolysis to excise the terminal mismatched deoxyribonucleotide
ATP-dependent formation of a phosphodiester bond between an adjacent 5'-phosphate and 3'-OH group
Binding of single-strand DNA-binding proteins to prevent nuclease degradation of the nick
q.p: Step 1 (Lagging strand Okazaki fragments have had primers removed and gaps filled by DNA Pol I, but remain unjoined due to a defect in DNA ligase) -> Step 2 (DNA ligase joins Okazaki fragments by catalyzing the ATP-dependent formation of a phosphodiester bond between the 5'-phosphate and 3'-OH on the DNA chain).

r.A: A ribonucleoprotein RNA template describes telomerase in eukaryotes, whereas joining Okazaki fragments in E. coli requires DNA ligase.
r.B: Incoming dNTPs with pyrophosphate release are used by DNA polymerases during chain elongation, whereas DNA ligase seals existing nicks where no nucleotide is missing.
r.C: 3' to 5' exonuclease hydrolysis is used by DNA polymerases I, II, and III for proofreading, not for sealing nicks between completed Okazaki fragments.
r.E: Single-strand DNA-binding proteins protect unwound single-stranded templates at the replication fork, whereas sealing double-stranded nicks requires ATP-dependent DNA ligase.

q.s: Slide 18-21: RNA Primer Excision, Gap Filling & DNA Ligation

q.v: In an experiment measuring the kinetics of bacterial DNA replication, a biochemist notes that although leading strand synthesis is continuous toward the replication fork and lagging strand synthesis is discontinuous away from the fork, both strands are synthesized at the exact same overall velocity. Structural imaging of the active replication fork reveals that the lagging-strand template loops back through a large multi-protein assembly. Which of the following components within this assembly directly tethers the core DNA polymerases to the DNA template to maintain this coordinated, simultaneous synthesis?
o: Initiator proteins bound to the A:T-rich origin
DNA gyrase positioned ahead of the replication fork
The sliding clamp within the replisome complex
DNA polymerase II repair complexes
Telomeric T-loop structures
q.p: Step 1 (Leading and lagging strand synthesis are kept going at the same speed by assembling the polymerases working on both strands into a large complex called a replisome) -> Step 2 (Within the replisome diagram, the sliding clamp is directly associated with the DNA polymerases and the looped lagging strand/leading strand templates to coordinate synthesis).

r.A: Initiator proteins bind at specific sites in the origin only to initiate local opening of the double helix, not to coordinate ongoing elongation speed at the fork.
r.B: DNA gyrase is a topoisomerase that works ahead of the replication fork to relieve positive supercoiling, rather than tethering polymerases together.
r.D: DNA polymerase II functions in DNA repair rather than coordinating leading and lagging strand synthesis within the replisome.
r.E: T-loops are protective structures at the ends of linear eukaryotic chromosomes (telomeres) and are absent from circular prokaryotic replisomes.

q.s: Slide 23: Coordinating Leading and Lagging Strands Synthesis

q.v: A 29-year-old immunocompromised male presents with painful, recurrent mucocutaneous vesicular lesions caused by Herpes simplex virus (HSV). Viral sensitivity testing demonstrates complete resistance to nucleoside-based therapies such as acyclovir and valacyclovir. The patient is started on a recently developed antiviral agent, pritelivir, which successfully halts viral replication and resolves the lesions. What is the specific mechanism of action of this effective alternative medication?
o: It is phosphorylated to a triphosphate form that lacks a 3'-OH group and terminates viral DNA chain elongation
It binds to the DNA/gyrase complex ahead of the replication fork to prevent the relief of positive supercoils
It stabilizes the interaction of the viral helicase-primase complex with the viral DNA substrate to inhibit replication progression
It degrades single-strand DNA-binding proteins, exposing the unwound viral template to host nucleases
It inhibits viral telomerase reverse transcriptase, leading to progressive shortening of the viral genome
q.p: Step 1 (Patient has acyclovir-resistant HSV treated with pritelivir, a helicase-primase inhibitor) -> Step 2 (HSV helicase-primase inhibitors stabilize the interaction of the helicase-primase complex with the viral DNA substrate, thereby inhibiting the progression of viral DNA replication).

r.A: Phosphorylation to a triphosphate nucleoside analog that terminates chain elongation describes AZT or acyclovir/valacyclovir, to which this patient's virus is resistant.
r.B: Binding to the DNA/gyrase complex to block supercoil relief is the mechanism of fluoroquinolone antibiotics (e.g., ciprofloxacin) in bacteria like E. coli.
r.D: Single-strand DNA-binding proteins (such as ICP8 in the HSV diagram) protect single-stranded DNA from nucleases, but pritelivir specifically targets the UL5/UL8/UL52 helicase-primase complex.
r.E: Telomerase inhibitors limit eukaryotic cancer cell proliferation, whereas HSV replication progression is blocked by stabilizing the viral helicase-primase complex on DNA.

q.s: Slide 25: Components of the replication complex & Slide 26: Clinical correlation (HSV helicase-primase inhibitors)

q.v: A comparative genomics researcher is analyzing the structural and enzymatic differences between DNA replication in human somatic cells and Escherichia coli. While both organisms utilize the same fundamental types of replication enzymes and semi-discontinuous pathways, the human genome is measured in gigabases (Gb) rather than kilobases (kb) and is packaged with histone proteins. Because human chromosomes are linear rather than circular, what specific structural problem arises exclusively at the extreme ends of the human chromosomes during standard S-phase replication?
o: Positive supercoils cannot be relieved because linear chromosomes lack a topological anchor for topoisomerases
DNA ligase cannot function at chromosome ends due to the absence of deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates
After removal of the terminal RNA primer on the lagging strand, there is no upstream 3'-OH available to prime DNA synthesis to fill the resulting gap
Initiator proteins cannot melt the terminal double helix because human chromosome ends are composed exclusively of A:T repeats
Single-strand DNA-binding proteins permanently fuse the leading and lagging strands together at the replication terminus
q.p: Step 1 (Eukaryotic chromosomes are linear and have telomeres, creating the 'end-replication' problem) -> Step 2 (At the telomeres on the lagging strand, once the terminal RNA primer is removed, there is no place upstream to synthesize a primer that would provide a 3'-OH to allow the daughter strand to be completed, causing progressive shortening).

r.A: Topoisomerases relieve coiling in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic replication; the end-replication problem is caused by the inability to prime the extreme 3' end of the lagging strand template.
r.B: DNA ligase joins internal Okazaki fragments using ATP, whereas the terminal gap at the telomere cannot even be synthesized by DNA polymerase due to the lack of an upstream primer.
r.D: Human telomeres are composed of short G-rich repetitive sequences (TTAGGG)n rather than A:T repeats, and the problem is primer placement for lagging strand completion, not origin melting.
r.E: Chromosome ends are protected from fusion and degradation by a telomeric loop structure ('T loop'), not fused by single-strand DNA-binding proteins.

q.s: Slide 28: Eukaryotic DNA Replication, Slide 29: The 'End-Replication' Problem & Slide 30: Telomeres

q.v: In 1996, the sheep 'Dolly' became the world's first animal cloned from an adult somatic cell using genetic material harvested from a 6-year-old ewe. Cytogenetic analysis of Dolly shortly after birth revealed that her chromosomes were 'old' at birth, exhibiting telomeres that were approximately 20% shorter than those of age-matched control sheep (19 kb vs. 22 kb). Which of the following best explains why this chromosomal abnormality was present at birth?
o: Adult somatic donor cells do not express telomerase, and the required in vitro laboratory cell culture prior to cloning further shortened the telomeres
The cloning procedure inactivated histone proteins, exposing the T-loops to rapid 5' to 3' exonuclease degradation by DNA polymerase I
Sheep chromosomes lack the repetitive (TTAGGG)n sequences needed for RNA primase to initiate leading-strand synthesis
Dolly inherited a congenital X-linked mutation in the telomerase ribonucleoprotein gene from the 6-year-old donor ewe
High levels of telomerase reverse transcriptase in the cultured somatic cells caused premature fusion of the chromosome ends
q.p: Step 1 (Dolly was cloned from an adult somatic cell of a 6-year-old ewe and had 20% shorter telomeres at birth) -> Step 2 (Most somatic cells do not express telomerase so telomere length reflects the 'age' of the donor cell, and cloning technology requires cells to be cultured in the laboratory for a period of time, which further reduces telomere length).

r.B: Telomere shortening in Dolly resulted from normal end-replication attrition in telomerase-negative adult somatic cells and laboratory culture, not histone inactivation or prokaryotic DNA Pol I activity.
r.C: The end-replication problem affects lagging-strand synthesis at telomeres, and Dolly's shortened telomeres were due to using aged adult somatic cells that lack telomerase expression.
r.D: Dolly did not have a genetic disease like dyskeratosis congenita; rather, normal adult somatic cells naturally lack telomerase activity and had already undergone 6 years of division plus lab culture.
r.E: Somatic cells lack telomerase expression, and when telomerase is active, it lengthens telomeres and protects against chromosome fusion rather than causing it.

q.s: Slide 31: Telomerase & Slide 33: The Life of Dolly

q.v: A 16-year-old male is evaluated in a medical genetics clinic for progressive shortness of breath, chronic diarrhea, and pancytopenia. Physical examination reveals patchy scalp alopecia, whitish plaques on his buccal mucosa, reticulated skin hyperpigmentation, dystrophic fingernails, and testicular atrophy. Genetic testing confirms a mutation in a gene responsible for maintaining the (TTAGGG)n repeats at the ends of his chromosomes. The pulmonary abnormality causing this patient's dyspnea directly results from a defect in which of the following telomerase-expressing precursor cell populations?
o: Ciliated pseudostratified columnar cells of the bronchi
Type 1 alveolar squamous epithelial cells
Type 2 alveolar epithelial cells
Pulmonary capillary endothelial progenitor cells
Interstitial lung fibroblasts
q.p: Step 1 (The patient has dyskeratosis congenita, a genetic disease of telomere maintenance resulting in reduced telomerase activity in highly proliferative tissues, presenting with alopecia, oral leukoplakia, nail dystrophy, marrow failure, and lung fibrosis) -> Step 2 (According to the dyskeratosis congenita organ system table, the lung defect [fibrosis] specifically affects 'Type 2 alveolar epithelial cells', which normally express telomerase).

r.A: The lecture material specifically identifies Type 2 alveolar epithelial cells, rather than bronchial ciliated cells, as the telomerase-expressing precursor cells affected in the lungs in dyskeratosis congenita.
r.B: Type 2 alveolar epithelial cells, not Type 1 squamous cells, are the proliferating pulmonary precursor cells that express telomerase and lead to fibrosis when defective in dyskeratosis congenita.
r.D: While bone marrow progenitor stem cells fail to produce blood cells in dyskeratosis congenita, the pulmonary fibrosis is specifically attributed to defective Type 2 alveolar epithelial cells.
r.E: Although fibrosis is the resulting clinical defect in the lungs, the underlying telomerase-expressing precursor cells affected by the mutation are the Type 2 alveolar epithelial cells.

q.s: Slide 30: Telomeres & Slide 35: Clinical correlation (Dyskeratosis congenita)

q.v: A researcher is tracking the inheritance of genomic DNA in a culture of proliferating cells from a 34-year-old donor. All parental DNA molecules in the initial G1 phase are uniformly labeled with a heavy nitrogen isotope, and the cells are then transferred to a medium containing only light nitrogen for a single S phase. Before mitosis begins, the newly replicated DNA duplexes are isolated and analyzed. Which of the following best describes the composition of each resulting double-stranded DNA molecule?
o: One heavy parental strand paired with one newly synthesized light daughter strand
Two newly synthesized light daughter strands paired together in half of the duplexes
Randomly interspersed heavy and light segments within both strands of every duplex
Two original heavy parental strands reannealed together after serving as templates
Single-stranded light daughter molecules that remain unannealed until cytokinesis
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that DNA replication occurs during S phase via a semi-conservative mechanism) -> Step 2 (Conclude that after one round of replication, each replicated molecule contains one original parental strand and one newly synthesized complementary daughter strand).

r.B: This describes conservative replication, whereas DNA replication is strictly semi-conservative with each duplex retaining one parental strand.
r.C: This describes dispersive replication, which does not occur because each intact parental strand serves as a continuous template for a complementary daughter strand.
r.D: Parental strands do not reanneal to each other after replication; instead, each remains paired with its newly synthesized complementary daughter strand.
r.E: Synthesized daughter strands are immediately base-paired in an anti-parallel orientation to their respective parental template strands during S phase.

q.s: Slide 3 (Cell Cycle) & Slide 4 (DNA Replication Overview)

q.v: A 42-year-old female presents with fever and flank pain, and a urine culture isolates Escherichia coli. In a research laboratory studying the replication kinetics of this bacterial isolate, investigators map the progression of DNA synthesis starting from the A:T-rich replication origin. After initiator proteins mediate local opening of the double helix at this site, how does chromosomal synthesis proceed to generate two circular daughter DNA molecules?
o: Unidirectionally from a single replication fork moving clockwise around the chromosome
Simultaneously from hundreds of distinct origins scattered across the circular genome
Bidirectionally with synthesis occurring simultaneously at two opposing replication forks
Sequentially by synthesizing the entire leading strand before initiating the lagging strand
Linearly toward terminal T-loop structures that prevent chromosome end fusion
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the process of replication initiation in prokaryotes like E. coli at a single A:T-rich origin) -> Step 2 (Deduce that strand separation creates two replication forks and replication proceeds bi-directionally at both forks).

r.A: Prokaryotic DNA replication is bi-directional and occurs at both replication forks rather than unidirectionally at a single fork.
r.B: E. coli DNA is replicated from a single origin of replication, whereas multiple origins are a feature of eukaryotic genomes.
r.D: Leading and lagging strand synthesis are coordinated simultaneously within the replisome so that both strands are synthesized at the same speed.
r.E: E. coli chromosomes are circular and lack linear ends or T-loop telomeric structures, which are specific to eukaryotic chromosomes.

q.s: Slide 5 (Initiation of Replication: Prokaryotes)

q.v: In a cell-free biochemical assay modeling DNA chain elongation, a template DNA strand hybridized to a short RNA primer is incubated with purified DNA polymerase and radioactively labeled deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs). As the enzyme extends the daughter strand in the 5' to 3' direction, a new phosphodiester bond is formed for each nucleotide incorporated. Which of the following specific chemical events directly drives the formation of this bond?
o: Nucleophilic attack of the incoming dNTP 3'-OH group on the 5'-phosphate of the primer strand
ATP hydrolysis by DNA polymerase to activate the 5'-phosphate terminus of the growing chain
Nucleophilic attack of the 3'-OH terminus of the growing chain on the innermost phosphate of the incoming dNTP
Cleavage of the terminal 3'-OH group from the primer to allow pyrophosphate attachment
Transfer of a ribose sugar group from RNA primase onto the 3' end of the template strand
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the mechanism of DNA polymerase-catalyzed chain elongation) -> Step 2 (Determine that the 3'-OH terminus of the growing DNA chain performs a nucleophilic attack on the innermost phosphate group of an incoming dNTP, releasing pyrophosphate).

r.A: The nucleophilic attack is carried out by the 3'-OH terminus of the growing primer strand, not the 3'-OH of the incoming dNTP.
r.B: DNA polymerase uses incoming dNTPs as precursors and releases a pyrophosphate group, whereas ATP-dependent phosphodiester bond formation is the mechanism of DNA ligase.
r.D: The 3'-OH group on the primer is required to initiate the nucleophilic attack and is not cleaved off to attach pyrophosphate.
r.E: RNA primase synthesizes a short RNA primer to provide a free 3'-OH group, rather than transferring a sugar onto the template strand.

q.s: Slide 13 (Chain Elongation)

q.v: A researcher is characterizing the enzymatic properties of purified bacterial DNA polymerases in vitro. A specific polymerase is isolated that functions primarily in DNA repair rather than bulk chromosomal replication or RNA primer excision. When this enzyme is incubated with a DNA duplex containing a mismatched base pair at the 3' terminus of the newly synthesized strand, it removes the incorrect nucleotide before resuming 5' to 3' synthesis. Which of the following profiles correctly pairs this specific enzyme with its exonuclease capability?
o: DNA polymerase I — 5' to 3' exonuclease activity only
DNA polymerase II — 3' to 5' exonuclease activity only
DNA polymerase II — both 3' to 5' and 5' to 3' exonuclease activities
DNA polymerase III — 5' to 3' exonuclease activity only
DNA polymerase III — both 3' to 5' and 5' to 3' exonuclease activities
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the prokaryotic polymerase dedicated solely to DNA repair as DNA Pol II) -> Step 2 (Match DNA Pol II to its specific exonuclease profile, which is 3' to 5' exonuclease activity for proofreading without 5' to 3' exonuclease activity).

r.A: DNA Pol I is involved in primer removal and gap synthesis in addition to repair, and it possesses both 3' to 5' and 5' to 3' exonuclease activities.
r.C: DNA Pol II possesses only 3' to 5' exonuclease activity; only DNA Pol I has both 3' to 5' and 5' to 3' exonuclease activities.
r.D: DNA Pol III is the primary enzyme for leading and lagging strand synthesis and possesses 3' to 5' exonuclease activity, not 5' to 3' exonuclease activity.
r.E: DNA Pol III only has 3' to 5' exonuclease activity and lacks the 5' to 3' exonuclease activity required to remove RNA primers.

q.s: Slide 11 (Prokaryotic DNA Polymerase) & Slide 12 (Proofreading)

q.v: In an experimental bacterial system, a mutant strain of Escherichia coli is engineered with a temperature-sensitive defect in a specific replication enzyme. When shifted to the restrictive temperature during S phase, RNA primers on the lagging strand are successfully excised and the resulting gaps are completely filled with complementary deoxyribonucleotides. However, alkaline gel electrophoresis reveals that the nascent lagging strand remains fragmented into short, unjoined segments. Which of the following biochemical reactions is directly impaired in this mutant?
o: Pyrophosphate-driven synthesis of short RNA primers complementary to the DNA template
5' to 3' exonucleolytic removal of ribonucleotides at the start of Okazaki fragments
ATP-dependent phosphodiester bond formation between adjacent 5'-phosphate and 3'-OH termini
3' to 5' exonucleolytic removal of misincorporated nucleotides at the replication fork
ATP-dependent unwinding of the parental double helix ahead of the replisome
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that successful primer removal and gap filling with persistent unjoined Okazaki fragments indicates a defect in DNA ligase) -> Step 2 (Identify the mechanism of DNA ligase as the ATP-dependent formation of a phosphodiester bond between a 5'-phosphate and a 3'-OH group on the DNA chain).

r.A: RNA primer synthesis is catalyzed by RNA primase early in replication, which must be intact since Okazaki fragments were generated and processed.
r.B: 5' to 3' exonucleolytic removal of RNA primers is performed by DNA Pol I, which is explicitly stated to have occurred normally in this mutant.
r.D: 3' to 5' exonucleolytic proofreading corrects mismatched bases during synthesis and does not join completed Okazaki fragments together.
r.E: ATP-dependent unwinding of the double helix is performed by DNA helicase to allow fork progression, not to seal nicks between Okazaki fragments.

q.s: Slide 20 & Slide 21 (DNA Ligation)

q.v: During an in vitro study of the bacterial replication complex, double-stranded DNA is incubated with initiator proteins, ATP, DNA helicase, RNA primase, DNA polymerases I and III, and DNA ligase. Although the double helix initially unwinds at the origin, the separated parental strands rapidly reanneal and are degraded by trace nucleases in the buffer before RNA primase can synthesize primers. Which of the following components must be added to the reaction mixture to directly prevent both premature reannealing and nuclease degradation?
o: Topoisomerase
Sliding clamp
Single-strand DNA-binding (SSB) proteins
Telomerase
Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs)
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the replication defect as the premature reannealing and nuclease degradation of unwound single-stranded DNA templates) -> Step 2 (Conclude that single-strand DNA-binding [SSB] proteins are required to bind single-stranded DNA, keep the strands apart, and protect them from nucleases).

r.A: Topoisomerases relieve coiling and torsional tension of double-stranded DNA ahead of the fork rather than protecting unwound single-stranded DNA from nucleases.
r.B: The sliding clamp associates with DNA polymerase within the replisome to maintain synthesis speed, not to coat and protect exposed single-stranded templates.
r.D: Telomerase is a eukaryotic ribonucleoprotein that adds repetitive sequences to the 3' ends of linear chromosomes and plays no role in stabilizing bacterial replication forks.
r.E: Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates serve as the substrate precursors for chain elongation by DNA polymerases rather than structural proteins that prevent strand reannealing.

q.s: Slide 25 (Components of the replication complex)

q.v: Karyotypic and molecular analysis of healthy human somatic cells reveals that the ends of every linear chromosome contain approximately 1,000 tandem copies of a short, guanine-rich repetitive sequence folded into a specialized loop structure ('T loop'). If a targeted experimental nuclease selectively disrupts this T-loop configuration without cleaving the underlying coding genes, which of the following pathological consequences is most likely to occur immediately in the affected cells?
o: Inability of initiator proteins to open A:T-rich origins of replication during S phase
Accumulation of positive supercoils ahead of the advancing replication forks
Chromosomal end-to-end fusion and recognition of the natural chromosome ends as broken DNA
Complete cessation of lagging strand Okazaki fragment ligation across the entire genome
Hyperactivation of 3' to 5' exonuclease proofreading activity by eukaryotic DNA polymerases
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the G-rich repetitive sequences [TTAGGG]n and T-loop structure at the ends of human chromosomes as telomeres) -> Step 2 (Determine that the function of the T loop is to protect chromosome ends from fusion and from being recognized as broken DNA and degraded).

r.A: Initiation at A:T-rich origins is mediated by initiator proteins internal to the chromosome and does not depend on the terminal T-loop structure.
r.B: Positive supercoiling ahead of the replication fork is caused by strand separation and relieved by topoisomerases, independent of telomeric T loops.
r.D: Ligation of Okazaki fragments is mediated by DNA ligase throughout the chromosome and is not controlled by the terminal T loop.
r.E: Proofreading via 3' to 5' exonuclease activity is an intrinsic property of DNA polymerases during chain elongation and is unrelated to telomere loop integrity.

q.s: Slide 30 (Telomeres)

q.v: A molecular biologist is investigating why linear eukaryotic chromosomes progressively shorten with each round of cell division in normal adult somatic tissues—a phenomenon known as the 'end-replication' problem. By tracking the terminal segments of the leading and lagging strands at the conclusion of S phase, the researcher observes a persistent gap at the extreme end of one daughter strand. Which of the following mechanisms directly accounts for the inability of standard DNA polymerases to complete synthesis of this terminal segment?
o: Eukaryotic DNA polymerases cannot unwind histone-bound DNA near the chromosomal termini
Removal of the terminal RNA primer on the lagging strand leaves a gap with no upstream 3'-OH group to prime synthesis
High G:C content in the telomeric repeats causes premature stalling of the replisome complex
Topoisomerases cannot bind to linear DNA ends to relieve terminal positive supercoiling
3' to 5' exonuclease proofreading erroneously degrades the final 20 nucleotides of the leading strand
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the 'end-replication' problem at linear eukaryotic telomeres) -> Step 2 (Conclude that after the terminal RNA primer used for the lagging strand is removed, there is no place upstream to synthesize a new primer that would provide a 3'-OH group to complete the daughter strand).

r.A: While eukaryotic DNA is associated with histones, the end-replication problem is specifically caused by the lack of a primer binding site at the extreme end of the lagging strand.
r.C: Although telomeres contain G-rich repeats, the incomplete synthesis is due to the inability to prime the terminal lagging strand rather than polymerase stalling from G:C content.
r.D: The end-replication problem results from primer requirements on the lagging strand, not a failure of topoisomerase binding at linear ends.
r.E: 3' to 5' exonuclease activity only removes mismatched nucleotides during proofreading and does not degrade correctly paired terminal sequences.

q.s: Slide 29 (The 'End-Replication' Problem)

q.v: A 61-year-old female is diagnosed with a rapidly proliferating metastatic carcinoma. Molecular profiling of the malignant cells demonstrates that, unlike the surrounding normal somatic tissue, the tumor cells have reactivated a specific enzyme that allows them to divide indefinitely without undergoing cellular senescence. A novel targeted therapy that directly inhibits this reactivated enzyme is administered. Which of the following biochemical processes will be most directly blocked in the tumor cells by this drug?
o: Synthesis of short DNA repeats onto the 3'-ends of chromosomes using an intrinsic RNA template
ATP-dependent unwinding of double-stranded DNA at viral and eukaryotic replication forks
Excision of RNA primers from lagging-strand Okazaki fragments via 5' to 3' exonuclease activity
Formation of phosphodiester bonds between adjacent Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand
Removal of positive supercoils ahead of the replication fork during S phase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the enzyme reactivated in cancer cells that allows indefinite division as somatic telomerase, and the drug as a telomerase inhibitor) -> Step 2 (Determine that telomerase is a ribonucleoprotein reverse transcriptase that uses its own RNA template to add short DNA repeats to the 3'-ends of chromosomes).

r.B: ATP-dependent unwinding of double-stranded DNA is the function of DNA helicase, not telomerase.
r.C: Excision of RNA primers via 5' to 3' exonuclease activity is a function of DNA polymerase I in prokaryotes during Okazaki fragment maturation.
r.D: Sealing nicks between Okazaki fragments via phosphodiester bond formation is catalyzed by DNA ligase, not telomerase.
r.E: Removal of positive supercoils ahead of the replication fork is performed by topoisomerases such as DNA gyrase.

q.s: Slide 31, Slide 32, & Slide 34 (Telomerase & Clinical correlation: Telomerase inhibitors)

q.v: An 18-year-old male with an X-linked genetic disorder affecting telomere maintenance presents for a comprehensive medical evaluation. He has a history of nail dystrophy, abnormal skin pigmentation, and bone marrow failure resulting from reduced telomerase activity in his progenitor stem cells. Based on the tissue-specific expression of telomerase in normal human organs, impairment of which of the following specific cell types directly accounts for the pulmonary and testicular manifestations associated with this patient's condition?
o: Type 1 alveolar epithelial cells and Leydig cells
Type 2 alveolar epithelial cells and spermatogonia
Ciliated bronchial club cells and Sertoli cells
Pulmonary capillary endothelial cells and epididymal principal cells
Alveolar macrophages and peritubular myoid cells
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the patient's disorder as Dyskeratosis congenita, which reduces telomerase activity in highly proliferative precursor cells) -> Step 2 (Map the organ-specific telomerase-expressing precursor cells responsible for lung fibrosis and testicular hypogonadism to Type 2 alveolar epithelial cells and spermatogonia, respectively).

r.A: In the lungs and testes, telomerase is specifically expressed in Type 2 alveolar epithelial cells and spermatogonia, rather than Type 1 pneumocytes or Leydig cells.
r.C: Bronchial club cells and Sertoli cells are not the designated telomerase-expressing precursor cells affected in dyskeratosis congenita.
r.D: Pulmonary endothelial cells and epididymal cells are not the primary telomerase-expressing stem/precursor populations whose failure causes lung fibrosis and hypogonadism in this disorder.
r.E: Alveolar macrophages and peritubular myoid cells are not the epithelial and germ cell precursors targeted by telomerase deficiency in the lungs and testes.

q.s: Slide 35 (Clinical correlation: Dyskeratosis congenita)

q.v: A researcher is tracing the incorporation of radiolabeled single-carbon units into newly synthesized purine nucleotides in rapidly dividing hematopoietic stem cells. After dietary folate is reduced to tetrahydrofolate (THF) via dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) and NADPH, a carbon unit from serine is transferred to generate the 5,10-methylene THF pool. To directly donate a carbon for the synthesis of the purine ring on ribose, 5,10-methylene THF must be interconverted into which of the following derivatives, and what is a key metabolic characteristic of this specific pool?
o: 5-methyl THF; it requires vitamin B12 to regenerate THF and is susceptible to metabolic trapping
10-formyl THF; it is reversibly interconverted with 5,10-methylene THF and is not metabolically trapped
Dihydrofolate (DHF); it is generated during thymidine synthesis and requires NADPH for reduction
S-adenosylmethionine (SAM); it requires ATP for synthesis from methionine and donates methyl groups to DNA
Carboxybiotin; it transfers carbon in the form of carbon dioxide rather than a methyl group
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the THF derivative required for purine ring synthesis as 10-THF / N10-formyl THF) -> Step 2 (Recognize from the folate pool properties that 10-THF is in reversible equilibrium with 5,10-THF and is not trapped)

r.A: 5-methyl THF (5-THF) is used for methionine synthesis rather than purine synthesis and becomes trapped in vitamin B12 deficiency.
r.C: Dihydrofolate is the oxidized product of the thymidylate synthase reaction (dUMP to dTMP), not the direct carbon donor for purine synthesis.
r.D: S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) is a methyl group donor synthesized in the SAM cycle for DNA, creatine, and catecholamine methylation, not purine ring synthesis.
r.E: Carboxybiotin transfers CO2 in carboxylation reactions (such as propionyl-CoA carboxylase), whereas folate derivatives transfer single-carbon units for nucleotide synthesis.

q.s: Slide 4 (Single carbon (1-C) transfers), Slide 6, and Slide 36 (Single Carbon Transfers via Folate Derivatives)

q.v: A 48-year-old man with a history of chronic pancreatitis and severe exocrine pancreatic insufficiency presents with progressive fatigue and paresthesias in his feet. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL, an MCV of 112 fL, and low serum cobalamin levels, despite normal gastric parietal cell function and an intact terminal ileum. Which of the following events in the gastrointestinal processing of dietary vitamin B12 is most directly impaired in this patient?
o: Dissociation of vitamin B12 from dietary food proteins in the stomach
Synthesis and secretion of haptocorrin by the salivary glands
Cleavage of the haptocorrin-B12 complex in the duodenum to allow binding to intrinsic factor
Receptor-mediated endocytosis of the intrinsic factor-B12 complex in the mucosal cells of the ileum
Binding of absorbed vitamin B12 to transcobalamin in the portal circulation
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that exocrine pancreatic insufficiency results in a lack of pancreatic proteases in the intestine) -> Step 2 (Determine that pancreatic proteases are required to degrade haptocorrin/R-protein in the duodenum so B12 can bind intrinsic factor)

r.A: Release of dietary B12 from food proteins in the stomach depends on gastric HCl and pepsin protease from parietal and chief cells, which are normal in this patient.
r.B: Haptocorrin (R-protein) is synthesized in the salivary glands and binds B12 in the mouth and stomach, a process unaffected by pancreatic protease deficiency.
r.D: Receptor-mediated endocytosis in the terminal ileum requires an intact ileum and prior formation of the IF/B12 complex, which cannot form if B12 remains bound to haptocorrin.
r.E: Transcobalamin binds and transports B12 in the blood after it exits the ileal enterocyte, downstream of intestinal lumen processing.

q.s: Slide 5 (Vit B12 Absorption) and Slide 26 (Vit B12 absorption)

q.v: A 3-day-old neonate is evaluated in the intensive care unit after a newborn screen returns abnormal and the infant develops severe lethargy, vomiting, and a dangerously low blood pH. Further genetic testing confirms a defect in the MUT gene encoding methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, and the clinical team initiates early dietary intervention restricting odd-chain fatty acids, cholesterol, and specific amino acids. Which of the following biochemical reactions is directly upstream of the accumulated methylmalonyl-CoA and requires biotin as a coenzyme?
o: Conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA
Carboxylation of propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA
Conversion of succinyl-CoA to succinate in the TCA cycle
Methylation of homocysteine to methionine
Conversion of THF and serine to 5,10-methylene THF and glycine
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the disorder as methylmalonic acidemia caused by defective methylmalonyl-CoA mutase) -> Step 2 (Trace the pathway immediately upstream of methylmalonyl-CoA to the conversion of propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA by biotin-dependent propionyl-CoA carboxylase)

r.A: Conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA is catalyzed by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase itself, which requires vitamin B12 rather than biotin.
r.C: Conversion of succinyl-CoA to succinate is a downstream TCA cycle step occurring after the methylmalonyl-CoA mutase reaction.
r.D: Methylation of homocysteine to methionine is catalyzed by methionine synthase, which requires vitamin B12 and 5-methyl THF.
r.E: Conversion of THF and serine to 5,10-methylene THF and glycine is catalyzed by serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT), which requires vitamin B6.

q.s: Slide 8 (Vit B12 Cobalamin), Slide 24 (B12-dependent Methylmalonyl CoA Mutase), and Slide 31 (Methylmalonic acidemia)

q.v: A scientist is examining the chemical structure of the vitamin cofactor required for both the conversion of homocysteine to methionine and the conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA. This vitamin is synthesized exclusively by a few species of microorganisms and must be obtained from animal sources or supplements in the human diet. Its core macrocyclic structure is chemically related to the porphyrin ring found in heme, but instead of iron, it coordinates which of the following metallic elements at its center?
o: Magnesium
Copper
Zinc
Cobalt
Manganese
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the cofactor required for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase as vitamin B12) -> Step 2 (Recall that the corrin ring of vitamin B12/cobalamin is related to the porphyrin ring in heme and contains cobalt)

r.A: Magnesium is not the central metal atom coordinated within the corrin ring of vitamin B12.
r.B: Copper is not found in the corrin ring of cobalamin.
r.C: Zinc is not the metal atom coordinated within the corrin ring of vitamin B12.
r.E: Manganese is not part of the corrin ring structure of vitamin B12.

q.s: Slide 8 (Vit B12 Cobalamin) and Slide 10 (SLO 2 Review)

q.v: A 64-year-old man with a history of chronic atrophic gastritis presents with mild fatigue. A routine automated complete blood count (CBC) reports a hemoglobin of 11.8 g/dL and a mean corpuscular volume (MCV) of 96 fL (normal: 80–100 fL). Despite the normal MCV, the clinician suspects an early vitamin B12 or folate deficiency and orders a manual peripheral blood smear count. Why might the automated MCV fail to detect this patient's underlying hematologic abnormality, and what specific leukocyte finding on the manual smear would confirm the suspicion?
o: MCV only measures reticulocytes; manual smear will show hyposegmented bilobed neutrophils
MCV is a calculated average and can miss early macrocytosis; manual smear will detect hypersegmented neutrophils
MCV is falsely lowered by elevated homocysteine; manual smear will detect microcytic red blood cell fragments
MCV cannot distinguish normocytes from macrocytes above 100 fL; manual smear will show giant platelets
MCV is only abnormal in intrinsic factor deficiency; manual smear will show atypical lymphocytes
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that B9 and B12 deficiencies cause megaloblastic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils) -> Step 2 (Apply the clinical pearl that MCV is an average and can be missed, whereas a requested manual count will detect hypersegmented neutrophils)

r.A: MCV averages all red blood cells rather than just reticulocytes, and B9/B12 deficiencies produce hypersegmented rather than hyposegmented neutrophils.
r.C: Elevated homocysteine does not falsely lower MCV, and microcytic anemia is seen when RBC building blocks are limited, such as in thalassemia.
r.D: An MCV >100 fL defines macrocytes on a CBC, but because MCV is an average, early or mixed populations can yield a normal value.
r.E: Both folate (B9) and B12 deficiencies cause elevated MCV (>100 fL) and hypersegmented neutrophils regardless of whether intrinsic factor is deficient.

q.s: Slide 12 (CBC can help differentiate anemias based on MCV) and Slide 13 (B9 and B12 deficiency will also result in hyper-segmented neutrophils)

q.v: An 8-month-old infant is brought to the genetics clinic due to failure to thrive, severe developmental delay, and recurrent seizures. Physical examination reveals marked microcephaly, and laboratory testing shows a macrocytic megaloblastic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils, despite normal maternal and infant dietary folate and vitamin B12 intake. Genetic sequencing identifies a congenital deficiency in dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR). Administration of which of the following agents would best bypass this enzymatic block by providing a downstream folate precursor?
o: Cyanocobalamin (Vitamin B12)
Folic acid
Leucovorin (folinic acid)
S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH)
Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP)
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that genetic DHFR deficiency blocks the conversion of Folate -> DHF -> THF, causing folate-deficiency symptoms plus microcephaly and seizures) -> Step 2 (Select leucovorin / folinic acid as the drug that bypasses DHFR deficiency by providing a downstream precursor)

r.A: Vitamin B12 is a cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, and cannot bypass a block in dihydrofolate reductase.
r.B: Standard folic acid requires functional DHFR to be reduced to DHF and active THF, so it remains ineffective when DHFR is deficient.
r.D: S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) is a byproduct of SAM methylation in the SAM cycle and does not replenish THF pools.
r.E: Pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) is a cofactor for SHMT and cystathionine beta-synthase, which acts downstream of THF formation and cannot bypass DHFR deficiency.

q.s: Slide 15 (Pharmacology), Slide 16 (Folate -> DHF -> THF), and Slide 17 (SLO 4 Review)

q.v: A 34-year-old traveler returning from a tropical region is diagnosed with malaria and prescribed proguanil. Within the body, proguanil is metabolized into its active form, cycloguanil, which selectively disrupts single-carbon metabolism in the protozoal parasite. Which of the following antimicrobial agents targets the exact same enzymatic step in bacterial folate metabolism as cycloguanil targets in malarial parasites?
o: Sulfonamide antibiotics
5-Fluorouracil (5-FU)
Trimethoprim
Folinic acid
Nitrous oxide
q.p: Step 1 (Identify from the slides that cycloguanil, the active metabolite of proguanil, specifically inhibits malarial DHFR) -> Step 2 (Match this mechanism to trimethoprim, which targets bacterial DHFR)

r.A: Sulfonamide antibiotics inhibit upstream de novo bacterial folate synthesis rather than dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR).
r.B: 5-Fluorouracil is an anticancer drug converted to FdUMP, which acts as a suicide inhibitor of thymidylate synthase.
r.D: Folinic acid (leucovorin) is a folate precursor used to rescue cells from DHFR inhibition rather than an inhibitor of DHFR.
r.E: Nitrous oxide is an anesthetic gas that inactivates vitamin B12/methionine synthase rather than inhibiting microbial DHFR.

q.s: Slide 15 (Pharmacology), Slide 35 (Case #6), and Slide 37 (Disruption of Folate Metabolism)

q.v: A 29-year-old woman with an unruptured left ectopic pregnancy and a 41-year-old man with severe plaque psoriasis refractory to topical corticosteroids are both managed medically with methotrexate. In the woman, serum beta-hCG levels gradually resolve without surgery; in the man, epidermal hyperproliferation subsides. Which of the following best explains why a single biochemical inhibitor is effective across both of these distinct clinical conditions?
o: It irreversibly inhibits thymidylate synthase via an FdUMP intermediate, selectively lysing trophoblastic and keratinocyte cell membranes
It competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, depleting THF derivatives required for purine and dTMP synthesis in rapidly dividing cells
It blocks the intestinal absorption of dietary folate in the terminal ileum, starving hypermetabolic tissues of methyl groups
It oxidizes the cobalt atom in vitamin B12, trapping 10-formyl THF and halting protein translation during the M phase
It inhibits cystathionine beta-synthase, causing toxic homocysteine accumulation that induces apoptosis in inflammatory cells
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the shared physiological target in ectopic pregnancy, psoriasis, and cancer as rapidly dividing cells / cell growth and division) -> Step 2 (Connect methotrexate's competitive inhibition of DHFR to the depletion of THF required for purine and dTMP/DNA synthesis, halting progression from G1 to S phase)

r.A: Irreversible suicide inhibition of thymidylate synthase via FdUMP is the mechanism of 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), not methotrexate.
r.C: Methotrexate is a folic acid analogue that competitively inhibits intracellular DHFR, rather than blocking ileal absorption (which is the site of B12 uptake).
r.D: 10-formyl THF is not trapped in B12 deficiency, and methotrexate targets DHFR rather than oxidizing vitamin B12.
r.E: Methotrexate does not inhibit cystathionine beta-synthase; it blocks the reduction of folate and dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate.

q.s: Slide 30 (Deficiency of THF derivatives), Slide 36 (Single Carbon Transfers via Folate Derivatives), Slide 38 (Cases #7 Methotrexate), and Slide 39 (Questions)

q.v: A 55-year-old woman originally presented with a hemoglobin of 8.5 g/dL, an MCV of 122 fL, and decreased sensation to light touch in her hands and feet due to pernicious anemia. She was placed on daily oral folic acid and oral vitamin B12 supplements. One year later, her hemoglobin has normalized to 13.0 g/dL (normal: 12–15 g/dL) and her hematocrit is 38%, yet over the subsequent 4 years her peripheral neuropathy and gait instability progressively worsen. Which of the following best explains why her anemia resolved while her neurologic deficits worsened despite taking oral vitamin B12 and folate?
o: Oral folate bypassed the 5-methyl THF trap to support dTMP synthesis, but oral B12 could not be absorbed without intrinsic factor to restore SAM and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase activity
Oral vitamin B12 was fully absorbed in the duodenum and corrected erythropoiesis, but excess folic acid directly demyelinated the posterior columns
Oral folate restored methionine synthase activity to normal, but failed to provide the biotin required for propionyl-CoA carboxylase
Oral vitamin B12 was inactivated by gastric HCl in the stomach, whereas oral folate was converted directly into S-adenosylmethionine in the liver
Oral folate corrected the deficiency of transcobalamin in the blood, but neuronal cells lack dihydrofolate reductase to activate folic acid
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that in pernicious anemia, lack of intrinsic factor prevents ileal absorption of oral B12, so the patient remains B12 deficient despite oral B12 intake) -> Step 2 (Deduce that high oral folate intake replenishes DHF/THF pools for dTMP/DNA synthesis to mask megaloblastic anemia, while unabsorbed oral B12 leaves methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase/SAM impaired, causing progressive demyelination)

r.B: Oral B12 is not absorbed in the duodenum and cannot be absorbed normally in the ileum without intrinsic factor; neurologic worsening is due to persistent B12 deficiency, not folate toxicity.
r.C: Folate supplementation cannot restore B12-dependent methionine synthase activity; it only provides fresh THF precursors upstream of the 5-THF trap.
r.D: Pernicious anemia is associated with parietal cell loss (low IF and often reduced gastric acid), and folate cannot be converted directly into SAM without B12-dependent methionine synthase.
r.E: Folate does not correct transcobalamin levels, and the persistence of neurological symptoms is due to failed ileal absorption of oral B12 requiring parenteral/alternative B12 replacement.

q.s: Slide 19 (High folate intake with B12 deficiency), Slide 32 (Consequences of Vit B12 deficiency), and Slides 40–43 (Case 8)

q.v: In 1998, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) mandated the fortification of enriched breads, cereals, flours, and grain products with folic acid, increasing mean intake by approximately 190 mcg/day. While this public health policy successfully targeted a specific developmental anomaly in utero, it also introduced a diagnostic pitfall in older adults with undiagnosed malabsorptive or autoimmune disorders. Which of the following pairs correctly identifies the primary congenital benefit and the potential clinical risk of this fortification policy?
o: Prevention of congenital microcephaly; increased risk of infant metabolic acidosis from methylmalonic acidemia
Prevention of fetal neural tube closure deficits; masking of macrocytic anemia and hypersegmented neutrophils in vitamin B12 deficiency
Prevention of downward lens subluxation and marfanoid habitus; induction of autoimmune antibodies against gastric parietal cells
Prevention of neonatal cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency; competitive inhibition of intestinal haptocorrin synthesis
Prevention of maternal deep venous thrombosis; depletion of hepatic vitamin B12 storage pools
q.p: Step 1 (Identify from the disorder table that folate deficiency in pregnancy causes neural tube closure deficits in utero, which grain fortification prevents) -> Step 2 (Connect high dietary folate intake to the masking of megaloblastic anemia and hypersegmented neutrophils in B12-deficient patients, allowing irreversible demyelination/neuropathy to progress undiagnosed)

r.A: Congenital microcephaly and seizures are associated with genetic DHFR deficiency, and methylmalonic acidemia is a genetic defect in MUT or B12 deficiency, not a side effect of folate fortification.
r.C: Lens subluxation and marfanoid habitus occur in genetic cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, and folic acid does not induce autoimmune parietal cell destruction.
r.D: Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency is a genetic disorder not prevented by folic acid, and folic acid does not inhibit salivary haptocorrin synthesis.
r.E: While CBS deficiency causes thrombosis, the primary public health goal of folic acid fortification in pregnancy is preventing neural tube defects, and folate does not deplete hepatic B12 stores.

q.s: Slide 18 (SLO 5 Table), Slide 19 (With high folate intake a person with B12 deficiency...), and Slide 44 (FDA folic acid fortification policy)

q.v: A researcher is studying the initial entry of single-carbon units into the tetrahydrofolate (THF) pool in rapidly dividing bone marrow progenitor cells. In a series of enzymatic assays, unmodified THF is incubated with serine to generate the N5,N10-methylene THF pool required for thymidine synthesis. Which of the following pairs of additional reactant/cofactor and amino acid product are directly involved in this specific reversible reaction?
o: Vitamin B6 (PLP) and glycine
Vitamin B12 and methionine
NADPH and dihydrofolate
Biotin and succinyl-CoA
ATP and S-adenosylhomocysteine
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the reversible conversion of THF and serine to 5,10-THF catalyzed by serine hydroxymethyltransferase [SHMT]) -> Step 2 (Determine that this reaction requires Vitamin B6 as a cofactor and releases glycine as the amino acid product).

r.B: Vitamin B12 is a cofactor for methionine synthase, which converts homocysteine and 5-methyl THF into methionine and THF.
r.C: NADPH is the reducing equivalent used by dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) to convert folate to dihydrofolate (DHF) and subsequently to THF.
r.D: Biotin is used by propionyl-CoA carboxylase to generate methylmalonyl-CoA, which is then converted to succinyl-CoA by B12-dependent methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.
r.E: ATP reacts with methionine to generate S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), which later yields S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) after donating its methyl group.

q.s: Slide 4 & Slide 6: Single carbon (1-C) transfers / SLO 1

q.v: A 42-year-old woman is evaluated for progressive fatigue and paresthesias in her lower extremities. Tracing the physiological pathway of radiolabeled dietary cobalamin reveals normal release from food proteins in the stomach, normal cleavage from salivary R-protein in the duodenum, and intact receptor-mediated endocytosis into the mucosal cells of the terminal ileum. After the intrinsic factor component is degraded inside the ileal enterocyte, the cobalamin exits the basolateral membrane into the portal circulation. Which of the following proteins must bind cobalamin in the blood to transport it to peripheral tissues?
o: Haptocorrin
Transcobalamin
Cholecystokinin-releasing peptide (CCK-RP)
Pepsin
S-adenosylmethionine
q.p: Step 1 (Trace B12 absorption past ileal receptor-mediated endocytosis and intracellular degradation of intrinsic factor) -> Step 2 (Identify transcobalamin as the specific B12-binding protein in the blood that transports B12 to target cells).

r.A: Haptocorrin (R-protein) is synthesized by the salivary glands and binds dietary B12 in the mouth and stomach before being cleaved by pancreatic proteases in the intestine.
r.C: CCK-RP is secreted by enterocytes to stimulate I cells to release cholecystokinin (CCK), which promotes pancreatic protease secretion in the duodenum.
r.D: Pepsin is a gastric protease activated by HCl from parietal cells that releases B12 from food proteins in the stomach.
r.E: S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) is an intracellular methyl group donor synthesized from methionine and ATP, not a plasma transport protein.

q.s: Slide 5 & Slide 26: Vit B12 Absorption / Case #2

q.v: A 68-year-old man with severe nutritional deficiency is found to have markedly elevated serum and urinary levels of methylmalonic acid (MMA) due to impaired activity of a vitamin B12-dependent mutase. In healthy hepatocytes, this mutase converts methylmalonyl-CoA into succinyl-CoA so that carbons derived from odd-chain fatty acids, cholesterol side chains, and specific amino acids can enter the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. Which of the following enzymes is directly responsible for carboxylating propionyl-CoA to form the immediate substrate for this B12-dependent mutase?
o: Methionine synthase
Methylene THF reductase
Propionyl-CoA carboxylase
Cystathionine beta-synthase
Serine hydroxymethyltransferase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the B12-dependent reaction as methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA) -> Step 2 (Identify the upstream biotin-dependent enzyme, propionyl-CoA carboxylase, that converts propionyl-CoA into methylmalonyl-CoA).

r.A: Methionine synthase is a B12-dependent enzyme that transfers a methyl group from N5-methyl THF to homocysteine to form methionine.
r.B: Methylene THF reductase converts N5,N10-methylene THF into N5-methyl THF within the folate cycle.
r.D: Cystathionine beta-synthase is a PLP (B6)-dependent enzyme that converts homocysteine into cystathionine/cysteine.
r.E: Serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT) interconverts THF and N5,N10-methylene THF using serine and glycine.

q.s: Slide 8 & Slide 24: B12-dependent Methylmalonyl CoA Mutase / SLO 2

q.v: A molecular biologist is investigating the 'B12 deficiency trap' in cultured human erythroblasts deprived of cobalamin. As intracellular cobalamin is depleted, a specific tetrahydrofolate (THF) derivative accumulates because it cannot be converted back into unmodified THF, ultimately starving the cell of other one-carbon donors. Which of the following enzymes directly synthesizes this trapped folate derivative from the N5,N10-methylene THF pool?
o: Dihydrofolate reductase
Thymidylate synthase
Methylene THF reductase
Methionine synthase
Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the folate derivative that accumulates in the B12 deficiency trap as N5-methyl THF [5-THF]) -> Step 2 (Determine from the folate cycle that methylene THF reductase catalyzes the conversion of N5,N10-methylene THF into N5-methyl THF).

r.A: Dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) catalyzes the reduction of dietary folate to dihydrofolate (DHF) and DHF to unmodified THF.
r.B: Thymidylate synthase utilizes N5,N10-methylene THF to convert dUMP to dTMP, generating DHF as a byproduct.
r.D: Methionine synthase is the B12-dependent enzyme that consumes N5-methyl THF to regenerate THF; its impairment causes the trap rather than synthesizing the trapped molecule.
r.E: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is a B12-dependent enzyme in the odd-chain fatty acid oxidation pathway and does not interact with folate derivatives.

q.s: Slide 9 & Slide 34: B12 deficiency trap / Folate and SAM Bicycle

q.v: An 18-month-old boy is evaluated for developmental delay, failure to thrive, and hypotonia. Laboratory evaluation reveals a macrocytic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils, markedly elevated plasma homocysteine, normal methylmalonic acid levels, and severely depleted S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) levels due to an inherited methionine synthase deficiency. In addition to DNA methylation and myelin maintenance, the biosynthesis of which of the following energy-storing compounds in skeletal muscle is directly impaired by the lack of SAM in this patient?
o: Succinyl-CoA
Creatine
Propionyl-CoA
Glycine
Thymidine monophosphate
q.p: Step 1 (Recognize that methionine synthase deficiency causes a downstream deficiency of the universal methyl donor S-adenosylmethionine [SAM]) -> Step 2 (Identify synthesis of creatine as one of the core physiological functions dependent on methyl donation by SAM).

r.A: Succinyl-CoA is a TCA cycle intermediate formed from methylmalonyl-CoA via B12-dependent methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, independent of SAM.
r.C: Propionyl-CoA is an intermediate generated from the catabolism of odd-chain fatty acids, cholesterol side chains, and VITM amino acids.
r.D: Glycine is generated when serine donates a single-carbon group to THF via the B6-dependent enzyme serine hydroxymethyltransferase.
r.E: Thymidine monophosphate (dTMP) synthesis requires N5,N10-methylene THF via thymidylate synthase, not methyl donation from SAM.

q.s: Slide 11 & Slide 18: B12 links Folate and SAM Bicycle / SLO 3

q.v: A hematologist is reviewing the automated complete blood count (CBC) parameters of three different patients presenting with pallor and fatigue. Patient 1 has a deficiency in dietary folate and vitamin B12; Patient 2 has glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency; and Patient 3 has thalassemia that limits red blood cell building blocks. Which of the following correctly matches the expected Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV) classification for Patient 1, Patient 2, and Patient 3, respectively?
o: Macrocytic (>100 fL), Normocytic (80-100 fL), Microcytic (<80 fL)
Microcytic (<80 fL), Normocytic (80-100 fL), Macrocytic (>100 fL)
Macrocytic (>100 fL), Microcytic (<80 fL), Normocytic (80-100 fL)
Normocytic (80-100 fL), Macrocytic (>100 fL), Microcytic (<80 fL)
Microcytic (<80 fL), Macrocytic (>100 fL), Normocytic (80-100 fL)
q.p: Step 1 (Associate each underlying disorder with its specific effect on red blood cell size as taught in the CBC differentiation slide) -> Step 2 (Conclude that B9/B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anemia, G6PD deficiency causes normocytic anemia, and thalassemia causes microcytic anemia).

r.B: This reverses the MCV findings for B9/B12 deficiency (which causes macrocytosis) and thalassemia (which causes microcytosis).
r.C: G6PD deficiency causes a normocytic anemia (80-100 fL), whereas limiting RBC building blocks in thalassemia results in a microcytic anemia.
r.D: B9 and B12 deficiencies impair DNA synthesis and prevent G1-to-S phase progression, resulting in large megaloblasts and macrocytic (>100 fL) rather than normocytic anemia.
r.E: B9/B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anemia, G6PD deficiency causes normocytic anemia, and thalassemia causes microcytic anemia.

q.s: Slide 12: CBC can help differentiate anemias based on MCV / SLO 3

q.v: A 61-year-old man receiving high-dose methotrexate for a neoplastic malignancy is administered carefully timed oral leucovorin (folinic acid) to rescue his healthy bone marrow and gastrointestinal mucosa from severe toxicity. Simultaneously, another patient in the clinic is prescribed a combination of sulfonamide and trimethoprim antibiotics for a bacterial infection. Why is leucovorin able to rescue human cells from methotrexate toxicity, whereas bacteria remain susceptible to the combination of sulfonamides and trimethoprim?
o: Leucovorin directly oxidizes methotrexate into an inactive metabolite in the bloodstream
Leucovorin provides a reduced folate precursor that bypasses human dihydrofolate reductase inhibition
Leucovorin selectively activates thymidylate synthase in human cells while inhibiting bacterial thymidylate synthase
Leucovorin restores gastric intrinsic factor secretion to enhance cobalamin-mediated folate regeneration
Leucovorin acts as a suicide inhibitor of bacterial folate synthesis while sparing human dihydrofolate reductase
q.p: Step 1 (Identify that methotrexate inhibits human DHFR, blocking the conversion of folate/DHF to THF) -> Step 2 (Recognize that leucovorin [folinic acid] bypasses DHFR deficiency/inhibition by providing a downstream reduced folate precursor to replenish the THF pools).

r.A: Leucovorin is a folate precursor (folinic acid) that enters the one-carbon pool downstream of DHFR rather than chemically degrading methotrexate.
r.C: Thymidylate synthase is blocked by the FdUMP metabolite of 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), not directly activated or inhibited by leucovorin.
r.D: Intrinsic factor is a glycoprotein made by gastric parietal cells for ileal B12 absorption and has no role in bypassing DHFR inhibition.
r.E: Fluorodeoxyuridylate (from 5-FU) is a suicide inhibitor of thymidylate synthase, whereas sulfonamides and trimethoprim inhibit bacterial folate synthesis and bacterial DHFR, respectively.

q.s: Slide 15, Slide 16 & Slide 37: Pharmacology / Disruption of Folate Metabolism / SLO 4

q.v: During a pharmacology laboratory session, medical students compare the mechanisms of two anticancer agents, aminopterin and 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), on rapidly dividing tumor cells. Both drugs ultimately deplete intracellular deoxythymidine monophosphate (dTMP) and halt DNA synthesis prior to the S phase, but they act at different steps in the folate cycle. Which of the following accurately contrasts the immediate molecular action of 5-FU's active metabolite with that of aminopterin?
o: 5-FU's metabolite acts as a suicide inhibitor of thymidylate synthase, whereas aminopterin inhibits dihydrofolate reductase
5-FU's metabolite inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, whereas aminopterin acts as a suicide inhibitor of thymidylate synthase
5-FU's metabolite blocks methionine synthase, whereas aminopterin blocks serine hydroxymethyltransferase
5-FU's metabolite inhibits bacterial folate synthesis, whereas aminopterin selectively inhibits malarial dihydrofolate reductase
5-FU's metabolite prevents the conversion of N5,N10-methylene THF to N5-methyl THF, whereas aminopterin blocks purine ring synthesis directly
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the active metabolite of 5-FU as fluorodeoxyuridylate [FdUMP] and aminopterin as an anticancer folate analogue) -> Step 2 (Determine that FdUMP acts as a suicide inhibitor of thymidylate synthase [blocking dUMP to dTMP], while aminopterin inhibits DHFR [blocking regeneration of THF from DHF]).

r.B: This reverses the targets: FdUMP (from 5-FU) inhibits thymidylate synthase, whereas aminopterin and methotrexate inhibit DHFR.
r.C: Neither drug targets B12-dependent methionine synthase or B6-dependent serine hydroxymethyltransferase.
r.D: Sulfonamides inhibit bacterial folate synthesis, and cycloguanil (the active metabolite of proguanil) specifically inhibits malarial DHFR.
r.E: Methylene THF reductase converts N5,N10-methylene THF to N5-methyl THF; aminopterin inhibits DHFR, which secondarily depletes THF derivatives needed for purine and pyrimidine synthesis.

q.s: Slide 15 & Slide 37: Disruption of Folate Metabolism / SLO 4

q.v: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with acute unilateral calf swelling and pain confirmed to be a deep venous thrombosis. Physical examination reveals a tall, slender build with long extremities (marfanoid habitus), intellectual disability, and ectopia lentis (lens subluxation). Laboratory studies show a normal MCV, normal serum methylmalonic acid (MMA), and markedly elevated plasma homocysteine (↑↑↑). A genetic defect in the enzyme responsible for this patient's disorder directly blocks the conversion of homocysteine into which of the following molecules?
o: Methionine
Cysteine (via cystathionine)
Succinyl-CoA
S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH)
N5-methyl tetrahydrofolate
q.p: Step 1 (Diagnose cystathionine beta-synthase [CBS] deficiency based on lens subluxation, thrombosis, marfanoid habitus, intellectual disability, normal MCV/MMA, and ↑↑↑ homocysteine) -> Step 2 (Identify from the SAM cycle diagram that PLP-dependent cystathionine beta-synthase converts homocysteine into cysteine).

r.A: Conversion of homocysteine to methionine is catalyzed by B12-dependent methionine synthase, which causes macrocytic anemia and possible demyelination when deficient.
r.C: Succinyl-CoA is generated from methylmalonyl-CoA by B12-dependent methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.
r.D: S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) is the upstream precursor that is hydrolyzed into homocysteine and adenosine after SAM donates its methyl group.
r.E: N5-methyl THF is the methyl donor co-substrate for methionine synthase in the folate cycle, not the product of cystathionine beta-synthase.

q.s: Slide 8, Slide 11 & Slide 18: B12 links Folate and SAM Bicycle / SLO 5 Table

q.v: A 67-year-old woman with a history of gastric mucosal atrophy resulting from chronic peptic ulcer disease presents with progressive numbness and tingling in her hands and feet, a sore and inflamed tongue (glossitis), and severe fatigue. Peripheral blood smear shows large oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils, and bone marrow biopsy reveals large nucleated erythroid precursors that failed to progress from the G1 growth phase to the S phase. Because her hematologic disorder is specifically caused by a deficiency of intrinsic factor from gastric parietal cells, which of the following is the most precise classification of her anemia, and what concomitant metabolic profile is expected?
o: Pernicious anemia; elevated homocysteine and elevated methylmalonic acid
Pernicious anemia; elevated homocysteine and normal methylmalonic acid
Aplastic anemia; normal homocysteine and elevated methylmalonic acid
Normocytic anemia; elevated homocysteine and elevated methylmalonic acid
Microcytic anemia; normal homocysteine and normal methylmalonic acid
q.p: Step 1 (Identify the subtype of megaloblastic anemia caused specifically by intrinsic factor deficiency from gastric parietal cell loss as pernicious anemia) -> Step 2 (Conclude that the resulting B12 deficiency impairs both methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, elevating both homocysteine and methylmalonic acid [MMA]).

r.B: Elevated homocysteine with normal MMA is the classic metabolic profile of folate deficiency or isolated methionine synthase deficiency, neither of which is caused by intrinsic factor deficiency.
r.C: Deficiency of intrinsic factor causes pernicious anemia (a subtype of macrocytic/megaloblastic anemia) and impairs methionine synthase, leading to elevated homocysteine.
r.D: Intrinsic factor deficiency leads to B12 deficiency and macrocytic/megaloblastic anemia (pernicious anemia), whereas normocytic anemia is seen in conditions like G6PD deficiency.
r.E: Microcytic anemia is seen when RBC building blocks are limited (such as in thalassemia), whereas parietal cell/intrinsic factor deficiency causes pernicious anemia with elevated homocysteine and MMA.

q.s: Slide 18, Slide 28 & Slide 30: Decreased Vit B12 levels / Deficiency of THF derivatives / SLO 5
